In the darkness, his snout twitched. He remembered the poison, Vale’s calm eyes, Celeste’s frightened whisper, and Julian watching the photograph fall.

Then his hooves became hands.

His snout receded. The bristles vanished. His torn, sauce-stained tuxedo settled around a thoroughly human Detective Hartley.

He climbed from the dumpster with a lettuce leaf on his shoulder.

Captain Briggs waited at the alley mouth.

“You’re suspended,” he said.

“On what grounds?”

“Animal-related chaos. Destruction of evidence. Assaulting a buffet.”

“The buffet was obstructing justice.”

Briggs stared at him.

Ace wiped cocktail sauce from his cheek and looked toward the glowing gala windows. “Slick didn’t kill Ashworth.”

“And you know that because?”

Ace watched a siren’s red reflection pulse across the hotel glass.

“Because whoever planted that photograph wanted us to stop looking.”

chapters.title: Chameleon in the Precinct
chapters.text:
By midnight, the Seventh Precinct smelled of burnt coffee, wet wool, and the shrimp cocktail lodged in Detective Jasper Hartley’s left shoe.

“Suspended,” Ace told his reflection in the squad-room washroom. “Pending clarification.”

His reflection, wearing the remains of a rented tuxedo, offered no reassurance.

Chen stood in the doorway holding an evidence bag.

“Briggs said you could collect your things. He did not say you could interrogate the desk sergeant about secret societies.”

“I asked whether he’d noticed any sinister jewelry.”

“You asked him to remove his wedding ring.”

“It had a hand on it.”

“It had his wife’s fingerprint.”

Ace bent over the sink. Tomato-red water ran off his cuffs.

Chen set the evidence bag beside the basin and took out her phone.

“Here’s another problem. This is the original bottle. Seal intact since I bagged it at the tower. So whatever was in that hotel dispenser—”

“Was not an unfortunate coincidence.”

“No. Don’t touch this.”

Her phone vibrated. She glanced at the screen.

“Property clerk. Stay here.”

She stepped into the corridor.

Ace looked at the brown bottle through its plastic wrapping. HAND SATANIZER. Even the typography seemed smug.

He had lost his badge, his reputation, and possibly the deposit on his trousers. Somewhere, a murderer was enjoying the evening.

“You don’t get to be the only one who understands what’s happening,” he told the bottle.

He tore open the bag.

This was not an accident, he would later admit. The accident was believing that made it better.

He pressed the pump and rubbed the cold gel between his hands.

For one hopeful second, nothing happened.

Then his thumbs swung apart.

“Oh, that’s medically upsetting.”

His fingers fused into opposing bundles. His skin prickled green. The sink rose around him as though the entire washroom had begun standing up.

Ace tried to shout for Chen.

What emerged was a tiny, indignant hiss.

His tuxedo collapsed over him.

He struggled free of a sleeve and found himself on the basin’s porcelain lip, gripping it with feet that appeared to have been designed by a committee unfamiliar with feet.

A chameleon.

He could see the door with one eye and his own curled tail with the other.

This was useful, horrifying, and almost certainly against departmental policy.

Footsteps approached. Ace lunged toward the wall, expecting to fall, and discovered that his new hands disagreed. He climbed.

Below him, a probationary officer entered, surveyed the discarded formalwear, and backed out.

“I’m not doing another animal report,” the young man said.

Ace would have applauded his instincts, but his skin had just turned the exact beige of municipal neglect.

He went still.

For the first time all evening, nobody was looking at him.

Through the open doorway, he saw Dr. Ingrid Vale.

She stood beside the drinking fountain in a charcoal coat. The silk scarf was tucked beneath its collar. One pale-gloved hand held a phone.

“Yes, they’ve arrested Mahmoud,” she said quietly.

Ace’s tail tightened.

Vale glanced toward the squad room.

“The janitor took the fall nicely.”

His other eye swung toward her so abruptly that he nearly lost his grip.

“No. Don’t interfere.” Her voice sharpened. “The detective is burning through the vial. Let him finish the seven; then we take the Hand.”

A trolley rattled past, pushed by someone who was not Slick. Vale waited for it to clear.

“He’s vain, frightened, and determined to prove himself. You couldn’t devise a more reliable mechanism.”

Ace opened his mouth.

His tongue shot out and caught a drain fly.

He spent several appalling seconds reconsidering the wisdom of breathing.

When he looked again, Vale was walking toward reception, her phone already put away.

Chen returned carrying a property receipt.

She saw the clothes.

Then the opened bag.

“Hartley.”

From the wall, Ace gave a subdued hiss.

Chen closed her eyes.

“I left you alone for forty seconds.”

***

Reverting behind a mop bucket was an experience Ace would not recommend, particularly without advance warning to his knees.

Chen supplied his emergency gym clothes from his locker and stood guard while he dressed.

“Vale said seven,” he whispered. “And she said Slick took the fall.”

“You heard those exact words?”

He repeated the conversation. Chen typed it into her phone without interrupting.

“She was here giving a supplementary statement,” she said. “Briggs will have her arrival and departure logged.”

“Then we arrest her.”

“We establish evidence she can’t explain away. You being a listening lizard is going to challenge the affidavit.”

She sealed the bottle in a fresh bag.

“This stays out of your hands.”

For once, Ace did not object.

Captain Briggs intercepted them outside his office.

“I told you to go home.”

“Vale is involved.”

“And five minutes ago, an officer reported a lizard wearing your trousers.”

“Near my trousers. There’s an important distinction.”

Briggs held out his hand.

“Badge. Weapon. Now.”

Ace glanced toward Chen. She gave a small, unhappy nod.

The badge felt heavier coming out than it ever had going on.

“Your suspension is now in writing,” Briggs said. “No interviews. No scenes. No more animal-related chaos in my precinct.”

Ace handed over his weapon.

“May I at least apologize to the janitor?”

Briggs looked at the stained tuxedo hanging from Chen’s arm.

“Briefly.”

***

Slick sat in holding with his hands folded between his knees.

Without his mop, he looked older.

“I heard about the pig,” he said.

“Everyone heard about the pig.”

“Not everyone. My sister’s asleep.”

Ace sat opposite the bars. Chen remained by the doorway.

“Vale called it the Hand. She wants me to finish seven.”

Slick’s expression emptied.

“How many?”

“Five.”

The janitor lowered his head.

“Tell me the truth,” Ace said. No flourish. No threat. “Please.”

“I was an apprentice in the Order of the Hand. Before I learned floors were cleaner work.”

“The people with the pins?”

“Wealthy families. Judges. Bankers. People who think owning a city means they ought to own everyone in it.”

“And Ashworth?”

“One of them. Until he wanted out. He hired me because I knew what the bottle was.”

“You said you were taking it to a vault.”

“I was. To keep it from them until he could destroy it.” Slick looked up. “He was afraid they’d kill him first. He was right.”

“Vale?”

“I don’t know whose hand held the knife. I know whose orders mattered.”

Ace looked toward the bag Chen carried.

“Seven doses?”

“Seven. You’ve used five.”

Outside holding, a telephone rang unanswered.

“What happens at seven?”

Slick gripped the bars.

“The final squirt changes everything.”

For once, Ace had nothing clever to say.

chapters.title: Sloth on the Clock
chapters.text:
Slick’s janitorial closet had three rules posted above the mop sink:

**NO SMOKING.**  
**NO PERSONAL ITEMS.**  
**NO DETECTIVES.**

Ace Hartley had violated the third.

Suspended, disarmed, and wearing gym clothes, he sat on an overturned bucket between a vacuum cleaner and a crate of industrial sponges. The case files lay across the floor: Ashworth’s autopsy, gala photographs, building plans, and the security footage Chen had smuggled him on a thumb drive.

He reached for the ordinary sanitizer on the shelf.

His elbow struck an evidence pouch.

The pouch fell into his lap. Inside it rested the brown bottle with the horned hand and staring eye.

“No,” Ace said.

The bottle rolled. He caught it.

The pump depressed.

A cold drop landed on his palm.

His fingers shortened. His shoulders folded. His spine clicked into a curve, and coarse brown fur spread over his skin. The closet rose around him as his limbs lengthened and his gym shoes became distant objects dangling from his feet.

Ace dropped the bottle.

It took so long to hit the floor that he had time to regret every decision of his adult life.

The closet door opened.

Chen looked in. “Ace?”

He turned his head with painful slowness.

Her eyes narrowed. “You used it again.”

Ace lifted one long, furry arm.

“You’re a sloth.”

He nodded.

Chen stared at him for three seconds. “I’m going to count to three.”

Ace pointed toward the laptop.

His claw moved across the floor at the speed of a drifting continent.

Chen sighed and set the laptop down. “You have fifteen minutes before Briggs notices I’m gone.”

By the time she had connected the drive, Ace had reached the computer. The security footage showed a corridor outside Ashworth’s study. The timestamp read 11:47 p.m.

A janitor entered the frame.

Slick’s uniform. Slick’s cap. Slick’s broad shoulders.

The figure paused at the study door.

“Again,” Ace said.

Chen rewound it.

“Slower.”

She reduced the playback speed. The disguised janitor stopped beside the door and glanced down the corridor. Then the figure raised a hand and tugged a glove tight around the fingers.

The left hand.

Ace’s eyes, now strangely independent, fixed on the detail.

“Freeze it,” he said.

Chen did.

The image showed a pale glove, a narrow wrist, and a small movement of the thumb beneath the cuff.

“Slick is right-handed,” Ace said.

“He could have used his left.”

“He opens every supply closet with his right. Signs with his right. Scratches his left elbow with his right because he says his left hand has the grace of a drunk crab.”

Chen looked at the frozen image. “The killer wore his uniform.”

The figure slid a key card through the reader and entered Ashworth’s study. Minutes later, the figure emerged with something concealed beneath the coat.

Chen replayed the moment. “Vale.”

Ace nodded. “The left hand. The cufflink. The poison on her scarf. She framed Slick.”

The transformation began to fade. Fur receded, claws shortened, and Ace’s limbs returned to their familiar proportions. He collapsed onto the floor, human again except for his gym shorts and a powerful longing for lettuce.

Chen tossed him a cleaning smock.

“Slick will be offended,” Ace said, pulling it on.

“He’ll be offended you used his closet as a laboratory.”

“The laboratory used me.”

They hurried to holding. Slick stood behind the bars, gripping them with both hands.

“Tell me you did not use the bottle again,” he said.

Ace raised one finger.

Slick’s face tightened. “Six.”

“Accidental.”

“Your accidents have become remarkably consistent.”

Chen showed him the frozen footage. Slick studied the gloved hand and closed his eyes.

“Vale,” he said.

“You knew?” Chen asked.

“I knew whose orders mattered. Knowing is not proving.”

“What happens at seven?” Ace asked.

Slick glanced at the security camera before lowering his voice. “The Order calls it completion. The first six transformations strip away the surface sins. The seventh binds them together. The person becomes a vessel for the Hand.”

“The Hand meaning the Order?” Chen asked.

“Their power. Their will. Their claim over everyone they control.”

Ace looked through the bars at the Satanizer, sealed again inside its pouch.

“And if the seventh dose is taken?”

“It completes the curse,” Slick said. “Unless the person uses it with the right intention.”

Chen frowned. “That sounds suspiciously convenient.”

“Old magic is full of loopholes. The final dose can bind the vessel to the Order—or break the chain. It depends whether the user reaches for power or protection.”

Ace’s gaze returned to the footage. Vale’s gloved left hand paused on the screen, calm and deliberate.

“What counts as protection?”

“Using it for someone besides yourself.”

For once, Ace did not answer with a joke.

Chen gathered the files. “We need evidence that will survive court. The footage proves a disguised woman entered the study. It doesn’t prove Vale was inside the uniform.”

“Where does she keep the Order’s records?” Ace asked.

Slick’s expression changed. “Her private gallery. Beneath the public collection. Relics, ledgers, names, and a shrine for the vessels.”

“A shrine,” Chen repeated.

“The Order will be there,” Slick said. “If Vale has been waiting for the seventh dose, she’ll want the bottle in that gallery.”

Chen looked at Ace. “You’re suspended, disarmed, and one squirt away from becoming something worse than a sloth.”

“I’m aware of two of those things.”

“All three.”

Ace picked up the evidence pouch without touching the pump. “Then we don’t waste the last dose.”

Slick gave him a grim smile. “That’s what Ashworth said.”

Chen tucked the thumb drive into her coat. “I can get us inside Vale’s gallery tonight.”

“Us?” Ace asked.

“You are not going alone.”

Slick tapped the bars. “And if you’re entering a private gallery owned by the woman who framed me and murdered Ashworth, you’ll need a janitor.”

“You’ll need someone who knows which doors are real,” Ace said.

Slick nodded.

Outside, the precinct thundered with phones, footsteps, and shouted orders. Inside the holding corridor, the three of them leaned over the case files while the sixth dose faded from Ace’s blood.

The seventh waited in its brown bottle, quiet as a held breath.

chapters.title: The Janitor's Tale
chapters.text:
Slick waited until the holding-cell corridor emptied before beginning his story.

“Not here,” he said.

Ace glanced at the bars. “You’re in a holding cell.”

“I mean not where the walls have ears.”

“At this precinct, the walls have warrants.”

Slick reached beneath the cot and slid out a folded sheet of yellowing paper. Chen unfolded it across the bench. It was a hand-drawn floor plan of Dr. Vale’s gallery, with corridors twisting beneath the public rooms.

“You had this the whole time?” she asked.

“I had many things. Most were confiscated by people who don’t know the difference between evidence and personal property.”

Ace leaned over the map. “There are three galleries.”

“Three public galleries,” Slick said. “The private one is below them.”

Chen looked at him. “Start at the beginning.”

Slick’s usual slyness vanished.

“The Order of the Hand is older than this city. Seven families founded it around seven objects called Vice Vessels. Each one embodies a deadly sin.”

He nodded toward the bottle in Chen’s evidence bag.

“Hand Satanizer is the seventh. The first six transformations strip away what a person pretends to be. The seventh makes the truth permanent.”

Ace’s stomach tightened. “Permanent animal?”

“Permanent vessel.”

“That sounds worse.”

“It is. The Order believes a completed vessel can command people who surrender to their appetites. Bankers, judges, mayors—anyone with a weakness and something to lose. The city’s elite become handles. The Order holds them.”

Chen studied him. “And Vale wants the bottle for that?”

“Vale wants the bottle because Ashworth refused to give it to her.”

Slick’s scarred hands folded together.

“Ashworth belonged to the Order. Then he learned what they planned. He hired me to retrieve the bottle from a vault in Prague and hide it until he could destroy it.”

Ace blinked. “You were an international thief?”

“I was an apprentice.”

“You’re a janitor.”

“I contain multitudes.”

“Did you steal it?”

“I was supposed to. Ashworth had already taken it. He found me after that and asked for my help.”

“And then Vale killed him,” Chen said.

Slick met her eyes. “Yes.”

“Knowing and proving are different,” Ace said. “One is detective work. The other is paperwork, where justice goes to die.”

Slick tapped the map. “Tonight, Vale holds a private auction. Her guests will bid on art, relics, favors, and secrets. The real business happens below.”

Chen folded the plan. “We get the records and photograph everything.”

“And if we find the dagger?”

“We take it to Briggs and hope he remembers you’re useful.”

“I’m always useful.”

“You became a sloth in a mop closet.”

“An unusually insightful sloth.”

Slick gripped the bars. “Listen to me, Ace. The seventh dose is not a trick. Don’t waste it because you’re frightened. Don’t use it to save yourself. The Hand knows the difference.”

Ace looked at the sealed bottle. Its horned eye seemed to stare through the plastic.

“What if there isn’t another way?”

“There is always another way,” Slick said. “It may simply be more painful and less theatrical.”

By eleven, Vale’s gallery glittered with chandeliers shaped like clasped hands.

Chen wore a black dress borrowed from property control. Ace wore a tuxedo belonging to a detective twice his size. Its sleeves ended above his wrists, and the collar seemed determined to strangle him.

“You look like a waiter who discovered tax fraud,” Chen said.

“I look undercover.”

“You look upholstered.”

They entered through the service door while Slick pushed a cart of champagne toward the kitchen. He gave Ace one quick wink before vanishing behind a curtain.

The auction filled the main gallery. Bronze masks watched from the walls. A judge laughed beside a banker whose lapel pin bore the Order’s symbol.

Ace kept his hands visible. Every jeweled box and silver knife seemed to tug at his fingers. The raccoon itch returned.

Chen touched his elbow. “Focus.”

“I’m focusing on not stealing anything.”

“You’re sweating.”

“I’m dedicated.”

Their cue came when Slick dropped a tray.

Glass shattered. Guests shrieked. Music stuttered.

Chen slipped through a side door, and Ace followed. Behind a black marble panel, she found a concealed latch. The panel opened onto stairs descending beneath the gallery.

The vault smelled of dust, candle wax, and metal.

Shelves held bone masks, sealed jars of black fluid, an iron crown, and a wooden hand with pearl fingernails. On the far wall sat a binder thick enough to stop a bullet.

Chen opened it.

Names filled the pages: judges, council members, police commissioners, banking families, news executives. Beside each were debts, addictions, lovers, and other merciless notes.

“This isn’t a membership list,” she whispered. “It’s leverage.”

At the room’s center stood an empty stone shrine. Seven shallow circles had been carved into its base.

Above it, gold letters read:

**VESSEL VII: A CITY IN THE PALM.**

Ace felt the room tilt.

Then the alarm began.

Red light washed over the vault. Steel shutters slammed across the stairs. Three guards entered through a second doorway, weapons raised.

“Detective Chen,” said the tallest. “Put it down.”

Ace stepped in front of her. “Gentlemen, you’ve mistaken us for—”

Chen kicked his ankle.

He stopped talking.

The guards moved fast. One struck Chen’s wrist, sending her pistol skidding away. Another caught Slick as he came through the service passage and shoved him against a shelf. Bottles rattled.

Ace reached for the Satanizer.

A gun pressed into his ribs.

“Careful,” said a woman’s voice.

Dr. Ingrid Vale descended the stairs in a silver gown. Her empty cufflink hole had been filled with a black stone shaped like an eye.

She looked at the binder, the shrine, and finally Ace.

“Ashworth refused to surrender the bottle,” she said. “He thought destroying it would make him free.”

“You murdered him.”

“I corrected a betrayal.”

“You framed Slick.”

“He was convenient.”

Slick struggled against the guard. “You always confused convenience with loyalty.”

Vale smiled. “And now our detective has arrived with the final dose.”

Ace’s hand remained inches from the bottle.

Vale gestured toward Chen and Slick. “Use it.”

Chen shook her head. “Don’t.”

“Use it,” Vale repeated, raising her chin. “Or watch your friends die before the auction ends.”

The bottle gleamed inside its evidence bag beneath the red alarm light.

Ace heard his heartbeat.

For once, it did not sound like applause.

chapters.title: The Gallery of Vice
chapters.text:
The vault smelled of dust, gun oil, and money.

Ace stood beneath the inscription **VESSEL VII: A CITY IN THE PALM**, with three guns aimed at him and Dr. Ingrid Vale smiling as if she had won a dull auction.

Chen knelt beside an overturned shelf, her hands bound behind her. Slick sat against a cabinet, wrists cuffed, his janitor’s cap crooked. Between them lay the evidence bag containing the Hand Satanizer.

Ace stared at the bottle.

“Detective,” Vale said, “you have one remaining dose. You know what it does.”

“I know it gives me an unfortunate relationship with wildlife.”

“You have mistaken symptoms for purpose.”

“Peacocks, raccoons, snakes, pigs, chameleons, sloths. That’s a fairly committed symptom.”

Vale’s smile sharpened. “The Order of the Hand has spent three centuries refining the Vessel ritual. The first six transformations strip away a person’s lies. Vanity. Greed. Fury. Appetite. Concealment. Apathy.”

Ace glanced at Slick. “You called them sins.”

“I called them warnings,” Slick said. “There’s a difference.”

Vale gestured toward the binder scattered across the floor. Its pages listed judges, bankers, commissioners, and council members beside their debts, addictions, affairs, and fears.

“The seventh completes the process,” she said. “The vessel becomes an instrument. Every weakness is a handle. Through the Hand Satanizer, the Order can bind the appetites of others and steer them.”

“Give us a city full of handles,” Chen said, “and the city moves when you flex.”

“Precisely.”

Above them, beyond layers of stone and velvet, wealthy guests were bidding on stolen relics.

“And Ashworth?” Ace asked.

“A sentimental fool. He stole the Vessel and intended to destroy it.”

“He hired Slick to hide it,” Ace said.

“He hired a thief.”

“Former thief,” Slick corrected.

Vale ignored him. “Ashworth began contacting prosecutors and journalists. So I corrected his betrayal.”

“Stabbed him with a ritual dagger,” Ace said. “Poisoned him with the same substance on your scarf. Then planted the key card and dressed someone in Slick’s uniform.”

“Your frame job was elegant,” Chen added, “until the glove.”

Vale’s expression tightened.

Ace saw the whole chain: the silver **I.V.** cufflink beneath Ashworth’s desk, the left-handed figure tightening a glove in the corridor footage, the poison on Vale’s scarf, her calm interest in every transformation.

“Ashworth thought the bottle could be destroyed,” Vale said. “It cannot. It can only be completed or broken. Completion requires someone who has passed through all seven gates.”

“You’ve been watching me.”

“Of course. You were wonderfully predictable.”

“I am many things. Predictable is not one of them.”

“You sprayed yourself with the Vessel because you thought it was sanitizer. You used it again because you wanted answers, then proof, then your reputation back.” She tilted her head. “The seventh dose will give you what you have always wanted.”

Ace glanced at his torn tuxedo and chocolate-stained cuff. “A better tailor?”

“Glory. Authority. The right to be unquestioned. Use the Vessel, and the Order will make you indispensable. Refuse, and your friends die.”

Chen met his gaze and gave the smallest shake of her head.

Slick lowered his eyes.

Ace noticed his thumb moving strangely.

Not struggling. Measuring.

A thin metal sliver emerged from beneath Slick’s thumbnail. Ace remembered the janitor’s lesson: the best tools were the ones nobody noticed.

“Last chance,” Vale said. “Pick up the bottle.”

Slick’s hand jerked.

The display case behind him toppled with a spectacular crash. A porcelain mask shattered. Silver relics clanged across the floor. One guard spun toward the noise; another stepped backward onto a bronze bowl.

Chen kicked the bowl into his ankle. He fell.

Slick rolled sideways, snapping one cuff against the cabinet corner. The restraint sprang open.

“Janitorial safety violation,” he announced.

The remaining guard raised his weapon.

Ace slammed into the evidence table. It struck the guard’s knees, sending him into a rack of labeled jars. Black liquid sloshed as an alarm began to shriek.

Vale fired.

The shot punched through the table inches from Ace’s hand.

He dove across the floor and seized the evidence bag. With one desperate pull, he tore it open. The brown bottle gleamed beneath the red emergency lights, its horned hand and eye symbol staring up at him.

His skin prickled. Feathers seemed to itch along his shoulders. Greedy fingers, a snake’s cold patience, a pig’s appetite, a chameleon’s vanishing instinct, and a sloth’s heavy calm stirred beneath his skin.

“Use it,” Vale ordered, aiming at Chen. “Become whatever you need. Escape. Win. Be magnificent.”

For once, the words did not tempt him.

Ace remembered Slick behind the holding-cell bars.

*The Vessel listens for the hand reaching for itself.*

He remembered Chen helping him despite every ridiculous disaster, and Slick pocketing the fallen peacock feather instead of using it against him. He remembered mistaking admiration for usefulness.

The pump waited beneath his thumb.

Ace looked at Chen, then Slick, then the guards struggling among the relics. He did not want glory or authority. He wanted the people in this room alive—and the Order dragged into daylight.

“I’m washing my hands,” Ace said.

He pressed the pump.

A single dark drop fell onto his palm.

The vault went silent.

chapters.title: The Seventh Squirt
chapters.text:
The drop struck Ace’s palm.

For one breath, nothing happened.

Then the vault inhaled.

The alarm stretched into a single metallic note. Feathers burst around Ace’s face, blue and green beneath the flickering lights. His eyes sharpened, revealing every trembling trigger finger, every bead of sweat, every thread caught on Chen’s jacket.

“Not again!” he shrieked—in a peacock’s voice.

Vale staggered backward. “Yes. Take it. Let the Vessel open.”

Feathers collapsed into fur. Ace’s hands curled into paws, and every glittering object in the vault became irresistible: guns, jeweled masks, a banker’s gold watch. He lunged toward the nearest prize, chittering.

Scales flashed across his cheeks.

His pupils narrowed. The guards became threats, the weapons invitations. Heat filled his throat, and he coiled to strike.

Then he snorted.

His jaw broadened, his body swelled, and the scent of food overwhelmed him. Somewhere above, the auction’s untouched buffet called to him. He wanted to charge, chew, and devour everything.

A guard shouted, “Shoot him!”

Ace’s face rippled green. His features blended into the stone wall. For a moment, hiding seemed perfect. Let the others fight. Let the city burn without him.

Then time slowed.

His thoughts dragged through syrup. The vault moved at a sloth’s pace, giving him time to see what the bottle had shown him: the peacock, raccoon, snake, pig, chameleon, sloth.

Not monsters. Pieces of himself.

Vanity. Greed. Anger. Appetite. Concealment. Apathy.

He had blamed the bottle for every transformation, but it had only forced him to stand inside what he preferred not to see.

The sloth’s heaviness lifted. The masks fell away.

Ace stood human again, his suit torn and his hair singed. His palm bore only a faint red mark shaped like an eye. His mind, however, was clearer than it had ever been.

Vale stared. “What did you do?”

“Refused the promotion.”

The nearest guard raised his pistol.

Ace stepped aside as the shot cracked. He seized the guard’s wrist and drove the man’s elbow against the stone shrine. The gun skidded beneath a cabinet.

A second guard lunged. Ace hooked his ankle and let gravity finish the takedown. The man hit the floor with a grunt.

Slick, still working free of one cuff, smiled. “You can surrender, or I can explain how to remove blood from expensive carpeting.”

The third guard dropped his weapon.

Vale did not.

She snatched a ceremonial blade from the fallen display case and rushed Ace. He noticed everything at once: her weight favoring the right foot, the stiffness in her right shoulder, the knife in her left hand, and the dark residue on her cuff.

The poison.

The murder assembled itself in his mind.

Vale had disguised herself in Slick’s uniform and used the XIII card to reach Ashworth’s hidden floor. She had entered the study, stabbed him from the left with the poisoned ritual dagger, and lost her I.V. cufflink when he fought back. Afterward, she planted the key card to frame Slick, then paused at the door to adjust her gloves with her left hand.

Slick had found the body only after she was gone.

“Your mistake,” Ace said, catching her wrist, “was assuming a frame only needs to look convincing.”

Vale twisted, trying to slash his throat. Ace turned with her momentum, sent her shoulder-first into the floor, and pinned her wrist behind her back.

The takedown was so plain that, for a moment, nobody spoke.

Vale bucked beneath him. “You have no idea what you’ve destroyed! The Order owns judges, banks, half the city—”

“Good,” Ace said. “Then half the city can testify.”

Chen, still bound, gave him an exhausted look. “Could you untie me before the speech?”

Slick freed his remaining cuff and crossed the vault with a ring of keys that seemed to appear from nowhere. He unlocked Chen, then collected the fallen weapons.

A pounding began above them. Shouted commands followed. Police stormed the auction room, and officers poured into the vault. They disarmed the guards, secured the relics, and dragged masked members of the Order from behind their wealth and influence.

Captain Briggs arrived last, staring from the wreckage to Ace kneeling on Dr. Vale.

“Hartley,” he said. “Why am I not surprised?”

“Because I bring closure to every case.”

“You bring property damage.”

“Closure with property damage.”

Chen handed Briggs the evidence binder. Slick followed with the poison-stained scarf, the dagger, and the XIII card, each sealed in a clear bag.

“Try the evidence room this time,” Chen told Ace. “Not his desk.”

Ace looked toward the shrine.

The Satanizer lay on its edge. A crack ran through the brown glass. Then the bottle collapsed inward with a soft sigh, crumbling into gray dust across the seven circles.

The alarm stopped.

Ace listened to his breathing. No hiss. No snort. No chitter. No shriek.

Just breath.

He turned his palm over. No feathers, scales, or fur remained. Only a human hand.

Slick came beside him. “How do you feel?”

“Tired. Bruised. Human.”

“That’ll do.”

Chen, rubbing life back into her wrists, raised an eyebrow. “Don’t get used to it.”

Ace smiled. It was smaller than his old, dazzling grin and lacked its usual demand for admiration.

“No,” he said. “I think I’ll try to keep it.”

chapters.title: Clean Hands
chapters.text:
By Thursday, the seventh precinct had run out of interview rooms, clean coffee mugs, and people willing to say they had never heard of the Order of the Hand.

A banking chairman occupied the bench usually reserved for drunk tourists. A deputy mayor demanded a private telephone and received a public one with a sticky receiver. Upstairs, a police commissioner’s portrait had been removed from the wall, leaving a pale rectangle that everyone found unexpectedly cheerful.

Ace watched two officers escort a judge past the booking desk.

“Do you know who I am?” the judge demanded.

“Unfortunately,” Chen said, turning a page in her report.

The dismantling was less dramatic than the raid. It involved warrants, duplicated records, and investigators from outside the city arriving with sensible shoes. Chen had insisted on sending copies of the leverage binder to three separate agencies before anyone important could make it disappear.

Ace had once considered paperwork the place where adventure went to die. Now he corrected a date on his statement and kept going.

Across his desk lay the last pieces of Preston Ashworth’s death.

Lionel Voss had surrendered the tower’s maintenance records after discovering that loyalty to rich people did not include legal representation. Ashworth’s study door locked automatically when pulled shut. The supposed internal bolt, visible through the frosted panel, was decorative brass on an antique door.

“Six detectives,” Briggs had said upon learning this. “Not one of you tried the hardware.”

Ace had signed the supplemental report without offering an adjective in his own defense.

The poison had proved to be an old preparation from the Order’s collection, used to weaken victims quickly and give its punishments a supernatural reputation. The dagger had still done the killing. Vale’s scarf, cufflink, confession, and the footage supplied considerably more substance than any curse.

Celeste Ashworth and Julian Cross had been concealing an affair, not a murder. Ace found their embarrassment almost restful.

***

Slick’s exoneration arrived in a padded envelope.

Ashworth’s solicitor brought it personally: payment records, letters, and instructions naming Elroy Mahmoud as the man entrusted to remove the bottle from the Order’s reach.

One letter called him “the only employee in this building who notices what is actually happening.”

Slick read that line twice.

“Could have put it on a reference,” he said.

The letters explained his route through the tower, the bottle beside the dead man when he found him, and his panicked decision to carry it into the precinct rather than trust another wealthy patron. They did not make every choice sensible. They made his innocence clear.

Briggs apologized in his office with the door open.

Slick accepted, then pointed out that the holding-cell sink still leaked.

By Friday morning he was back behind a mop bucket, nudging a wet-floor sign into the path of a councilman’s lawyer.

“You could take a holiday,” Ace said.

“And miss this?”

Slick glanced toward the interview rooms and gave him a quiet wink.

Ace lowered his voice. “The hotel dispenser?”

“Vale’s people managed that gala. She wanted you reaching for the bottle without thinking. Chen found the refill instructions among the catering messages.”

“So I was being cultivated.”

“You were being predictable.”

There was no graceful answer to that. Ace settled for moving his shoes so Slick could mop beneath them.

***

The press conference took place under lights bright enough to interrogate a lighthouse.

Ace stood behind the lectern in a suit that no longer smelled of cocktail sauce. His bruises had faded to the color of elderly bananas. In his pocket, his returned badge felt heavier than before.

Briggs had reinstated him that morning.

“Medical clearance, completed statements, and no more livestock,” he had said, sliding the badge across his desk.

“I’ll do my best.”

“That was not a request for improvisation.”

Now cameras clicked. Ace recognized the familiar pause in which he normally assembled a sentence worth quoting.

He looked instead at Chen, standing beside the steps with a folder beneath her arm. Slick waited near the back, wearing his good work shirt.

“Dr. Ingrid Vale has been charged with Preston Ashworth’s murder,” Ace began. “Further arrests concern conspiracy, coercion, and offenses arising from the Order’s activities. Some people named in its records were victims. Their names will not be offered up for entertainment.”

A reporter raised her hand. “Detective Hartley, is this your biggest case?”

For a moment, he could almost feel feathers gathering between his shoulder blades.

“This case was solved because Detective Mara Chen kept investigating when I became”—he glanced at Briggs—“unreliable.”

Chen’s mouth twitched.

“And because Elroy Mahmoud risked his life to help us, after we had given him very little reason to trust us.”

The cameras swung toward Slick. He looked as though he would rather face armed guards again.

“My colleagues preserved the evidence,” Ace continued. “They protected people. I’m grateful to them.”

No dazzling conclusion arrived. He let the sentence stand.

Afterward, Chen joined him by the water cooler.

“Unreliable?”

“I considered ‘intermittently house-trained.’”

“Save that for your memoir.”

He handed her the revised report. Her name appeared first.

She noticed, but said only, “You missed a signature.”

***

That evening, the precinct resumed its usual noisy argument with the city. Telephones rang. Someone disputed a parking ticket with religious conviction. From the break room came the smell of scorched popcorn.

Briggs paused beside Ace’s desk.

“Where’d the old peacock go?”

Ace looked up. “Washed my hands of him.”

The captain grunted. “Keep the eyesight. Lose the speeches.”

When he had gone, Slick set a narrow paper envelope on Ace’s blotter.

Inside lay a single peacock feather.

“Thought you might want your property back.”

Ace turned it beneath the desk lamp. The blue-green eye caught the light, extravagant and faintly ridiculous. He remembered hiding feathers, inventing excuses, caring desperately who might have seen.

“Thanks,” he said.

Slick nodded and went back to work.

Ace placed the feather in his drawer beside the Ashworth files. Then he reached for the sanitizer Chen had left on his desk.

He stopped.

He read the front, the back, the ingredients, and the manufacturer’s address.

From across the aisle, Chen watched him.

“Satisfied?”

Ace laughed, pressed the pump, and rubbed his hands together.

Beyond the windows, the city glittered. Below that glitter lay leaking pipes, dirty floors, and people who knew which doors really locked.

Tomorrow, he would start there.

prompt: Create an original story set in a world where academic degrees grant literal superpowers and tenured professors rule as feudal lords. Follow a determined dropout who ignites a rebellion against the campus aristocracy and questions the true value of knowledge. Set the tale in a vast university-city blending medieval hierarchy with modern technology.

chapters.title: The Degree-Less
chapters.text:
By midnight, the Undercroft had begun to sweat.

Condensation gathered along the iron ribs beneath Veritas’s Great Library and fell in warm drops onto the streets below. Steam from the university’s boilers traveled through the pipes to lecture halls, laboratories, and the private towers of tenured professors. Down here, among rust and soot, the degree-less lived beside the machines that served their betters.

Eli knew which pipes were safe to sleep beside.

The blue-banded lines carried clean heat. The green ones carried water. The copper pipes beneath the library carried something that could blister bone. He knew which vents exhaled paper dust and which exhaled poisonous ink. He knew where scholars threw out broken chairs, cracked tablets, and half-eaten pastries.

Degrees taught people to command the world.

Being degree-less taught Eli how not to be killed by it.

He crouched beneath a maintenance grate, lantern between his knees, prying the brass teeth from a discarded citation engine. The machine had once stamped references into parchment with a graduate assistant’s seal. Now its gears were clogged with wax and hair.

“Come on,” Eli muttered.

The engine clicked.

“Thank you.”

It clicked again, then spat black sparks. One burned through his sleeve. Eli slapped it out and pulled the final gear free. The scrap brokers would pay enough for it to buy two meals.

Something skittered across the ceiling.

Eli killed the lantern.

Eight tiny taps. A pause. Eight more.

Proctor-spider.

It descended on a silver filament, its body the size of a hound, its eight brass legs ending in needle points. A parchment seal fluttered beneath its abdomen.

ACADEMIC INTEGRITY DIVISION.

Its single glass eye brightened.

“Unauthorized salvage,” it whispered in a voice assembled from recorded lectures. “Unlicensed intellectual activity. Present credentials.”

Eli pressed himself into the shadow beneath the grate. The spider lowered one leg and scraped the floor.

Then a bottle shattered in the darkness behind it.

The spider spun toward the sound. Eli crawled through the grate, dragged it shut, and ran.

His shelter lay three tunnels away, inside an abandoned cataloging vault. He slipped through a curtain of old index cards and crouched beside his bedroll, listening.

Nothing followed.

From inside his coat, he took the object he had found that afternoon: a long, toothless brass key engraved with a circle crossed by three lines.

He had discovered it in a box labeled OBSOLETE—FOUNDATIONAL MATERIALS beneath a collapsed shelf in the sealed eastern stacks. The key had no teeth, but when Eli touched it to a locked door hidden behind the shelf, the door opened.

Vault 0 contained no books.

There was only a stone table, a dead brass lamp, and a codex lying beneath a sheet of glass.

Eli had broken the glass with a chair.

The codex was bound in a pale material that felt neither like leather nor paper. Its pages were blank—not white, exactly, but emptied of color. They drank the lantern light.

When Eli touched one, black ink appeared beneath his finger.

WHAT DO YOU PERMIT?

He had pulled his hand away. The words remained.

“What are the Foundational Texts?” he had whispered.

The ink gathered into a second line.

WHO WROTE THE FIRST LAW?

“I don’t know.”

WHO BENEFITS WHEN A QUESTION HAS ONLY ONE ANSWER?

Eli had fled when alarms began ringing through the library.

Now, in the cataloging vault, he opened the codex again. The same words waited on the page.

PERMISSION IS NOT TRUTH.

Every child in Veritas knew the Foundational Texts were eternal. The Principles of Matter, the Axioms of Rhetoric, the Canon of Healing: all had supposedly been discovered by the First Chancellor and preserved by the university ever since.

A degree did not merely prove mastery. It opened the door to a Discipline.

Without one, a person could not shape heat, summon evidence, mend flesh, or persuade a locked gate.

Without one, a person was only Eli.

A bell clanged overhead.

Not the hour bell. The harsh triple alarm used during inspections.

Voices entered the Undercroft.

“By order of Chancellor Voss, all unauthorized residents will submit for examination!”

Graduate assistants poured through the eastern archway in gray robes, silver-threaded collars, and shining degree badges. One raised a hand. Blue fire raced along the pipes.

Eli snapped the codex shut.

The flames reached the cataloging vault. Index cards burst into fire.

He grabbed the book and ran.

A spell struck the floor behind him, buckling stone. Another transformed a pile of scrap into shrieking paper birds. Eli plunged down a service stair, coughing as steam blinded him. He slipped, struck his shoulder, and nearly dropped the codex.

At the bottom stood a riveted iron door with no handle or keyhole.

Eli shoved it.

It opened.

An old woman stood beyond it, holding a wrench like a sword.

Her white hair was braided down her back. Goggles rested on her forehead, and her oil-black coat was patched with colored thread. Behind her, a furnace glowed and a network of pipes crossed the workshop walls in careful patterns.

She looked at Eli, then at the burning stairwell.

“You’re late,” she said.

“I’m sorry?”

“If you’re going to bring the university down on my roof, arrive before supper.”

The assistants shouted above.

Eli lifted the codex. “I found this.”

The woman’s expression changed—not to surprise, but recognition.

She stepped forward and caught his wrist.

“What does it say?”

“It asked what I permit.”

“And what did you answer?”

“Nothing.”

Fear entered her face.

“Good,” she said. “Come inside.”

She pulled him into the workshop and slammed the door. With three turns of the wrench, she sealed the bolts. The shouting faded to muffled thunder.

“My name is Wren,” she said. “Master of the lower maintenance guild, though the university stopped recognizing the guild forty years ago.”

“Why help me?”

Wren looked at the codex.

“Because dangerous questions have been asked before.”

“What happened to the people who asked them?”

She took the book from him but did not open it.

“Some were burned,” she said. “Some were promoted. The worst fate is difficult to say.”

The furnace breathed behind her. Pipes trembled in the walls like sleeping beasts.

“Come,” Wren said. “You’ll need shelter tonight.”

“And tomorrow?”

Wren carried the codex toward the back of the workshop.

“Tomorrow,” she said, “we find out whether it has begun answering you.”

chapters.title: The Names of Things
chapters.text:
Wren did not sleep so much as change positions.

At midnight she lay beneath the workbench with one ear against the stone. At two, she sat beside the boiler, listening to its ticking. At dawn, Eli found her on the workshop roof, wrapped in oilskin and watching Veritas kindle below.

“Come up,” she said.

From the roof, the city rose in layers: the black chimneys of the Undercroft, the crowded tenements of the Commons, the bridges and lecture halls, and, at the summit, the Chancellor’s citadel shining like a coin.

“What are you listening to?” Eli asked.

“Everything.”

“That’s not an answer.”

“It is if you know the names.”

She took a brass-headed hammer from her belt and tapped the roof. Once. Twice. Three times.

“Furnace brick,” she said. “Soft in the middle, hard at the skin. It carries heat sideways when the weather turns wet. Beneath it is iron plate, patched with slag. The slag is tired. It will split before winter.”

“You can tell that by tapping?”

“I can tell because the roof answered.”

She handed him the hammer. Eli struck the brick. The note was hollow near the edge.

“Loose,” he said.

“Why?”

“Different pitch.”

“Again.”

He listened. Beneath the hollow note was a faint trembling.

“Water behind it.”

Wren nodded. “The city speaks before it breaks. People merely prefer the break. It is more dramatic.”

She led him down into the workshop and opened a cabinet he had mistaken for part of the wall. Inside lay hundreds of narrow wooden strips, each marked with a word in faded ink.

Wren selected one.

“Vey,” she said.

“What does it mean?”

“Pressure that wants out but has not chosen where.”

“That’s a word?”

“It is now.”

She placed another strip beside it. “Orn. Pressure trapped by a flaw in its vessel. Dangerous because it believes the vessel is the problem.”

“And this?”

“Kes. The quiet before a pipe bursts.”

Eli touched the worn letters. “You made these?”

“My teacher did. Her teacher before her. We carried the names in our mouths when the university began locking them out of books.”

“Why lock out names?”

“Because names let people work without permission.”

Wren opened the boiler’s inspection hatch. Steam breathed into the room.

“The Disciplines are not magic in the way professors claim. They are agreements. Old agreements, polished until everyone forgot they were agreements. A scholar recites the sanctioned name of heat, and heat obeys because the university has taught the world to recognize that voice.”

Eli thought of the graduate assistants, their silver badges, and the blue fire leaping from their hands.

“Then why can’t I do it?”

“Because no one gave you the words.”

“No one gave me the truth.”

Wren glanced at him. “Those are not always the same thing.”

Beneath the boiler she found a blackened slate. Carved into it was a circle crossed by three lines.

Eli’s hand went to the brass key beneath his shirt.

“You know it.”

“I know what it used to mean.”

“Tell me.”

“Before the university, knowledge belonged to whoever needed it. Millers knew grain. Masons knew which stones would bear a tower. Midwives knew the thousand differences between pain and danger. Not everyone knew everything, but knowledge traveled.”

She rubbed the symbol with her thumb.

“The first Chancellor gathered those people here. He called the university a commons and promised to preserve what was being lost. He wrote down their methods, warnings, and names. Then he discovered that a written thing could be withheld.”

“He charged for access.”

“At first, only for ink and instruction. Then examinations to prove who was worthy. Then degrees to prove who had passed. He said he was protecting knowledge from fools.”

“And was he?”

“Some fools were kept away. So were the poor, rivals, and anyone who asked who had appointed him guardian.”

Wren closed the cabinet.

“The Foundational Texts were assembled from thousands of voices. The university erased the voices and kept the commands: Principles of Matter, Axioms of Rhetoric, Canon of Healing. They became laws because the Chancellor declared them laws.”

Eli pictured the pale codex beneath its glass, blank until his hand touched it.

“What does it want from me?”

“Perhaps it wants you to stop asking what it wants.”

“That isn’t helpful.”

“It is the most helpful answer I have.”

A bell began ringing overhead. Not the measured bells of lectures, nor the bright chime announcing a successful defense. This was a harsh, repeating clang that seemed to strike the whole city.

Wren went still.

“Tuition decree.”

By the time Eli followed her outside, the Commons had filled. Students poured from the lower colleges in dark robes, carrying placards that flashed with projected letters: DOUBLE FEES, HALF MEALS. Adjunct lecturers marched beside them, credentials pinned to their coats like medals from a war they had lost. Artisans emerged from alleys and machine sheds. Someone had overturned a registrar’s cart, and enchanted forms fluttered through the air.

On the bridge above, mounted proctors formed a line. Behind them stood a dean in crimson velvet, his face enlarged by a speaking spell.

“Return to your assigned wards,” he commanded. “The revised tuition ensures academic excellence and protects the value of your degrees.”

A stone struck the bridge rail.

The dean’s smile did not change. “Further disorder will be recorded as evidence of unfitness.”

A girl near Eli raised her voice. “My brother sold his years for a degree! He still can’t afford bread!”

The crowd answered with a roar.

The proctors lifted their staffs.

Fear moved through the people—not sudden, but practiced. Students lowered their signs. Adjuncts stepped backward. The university had taught them that punishment proved order, and order proved truth.

Wren seized Eli’s sleeve.

“Come away.”

“They can’t just—”

“They can do exactly what they have always done. That is why they call it tradition.”

The first staff discharged. Blue light cracked across the street. People scattered on rain-slick stones. A boy fell, and no one reached him until Wren pushed through the crowd and dragged him behind a coal cart.

She pressed a cloth to his bleeding forehead and spoke softly in the old names: pressure, vessel, breath, bone. The words did not flare. They summoned no obedient miracle.

But the boy breathed.

Eli looked toward the Chancellor’s citadel. Beneath his shirt, the codex seemed to stir against his ribs.

A key, he thought.

Not a curse. Not a weapon.

A key asked what door a person had been taught not to see.

For the first time, Eli wondered whether the university’s greatest secret was not that its laws were false, but that everyone outside its walls already knew better ones.

chapters.title: The Broken Scholar
chapters.text:
The Infirmary occupied the oldest hill in Veritas. Its upper towers gleamed with healing sigils, but beneath the licensed wards and student clinics lay rooms the university did not advertise.

Wren sent Eli there at dusk with a brass token stamped with the maintenance guild’s old mark.

“Ask for the ward below the ward,” she said. “If they tell you there isn’t one, you’re close.”

“And if Kael doesn’t want to see me?”

“He hasn’t wanted to see anyone in six years. You’re not asking him to be well. You’re asking what he saw.”

The token opened a freight lift in a linen storeroom. Eli descended through damp darkness, past pipes furred with mineral crust. The lower ward smelled of iron, boiled herbs, and rain trapped in stone. Patients sat behind narrow windows, staring at things that were not there. One woman whispered the same sentence to an empty corner. A boy’s shadow moved half a second after him.

At the corridor’s end, a nurse barred Eli’s way.

“Authorized visitors only.”

He held up the token.

Her expression tightened. “That guild hasn’t had access here since the Chancellor’s grandfather.”

“Then tell me where Kael is.”

“Kael is not someone you visit.”

“Wren says otherwise.”

The nurse looked away. “Room nine. Don’t touch him. Don’t answer if he asks a question.”

“Why?”

“The last person who did spent three weeks believing she was a staircase.”

Room nine had no bed. Kael sat on the floor with his back against the wall, knees drawn to his chest. He was younger than Eli expected, perhaps thirty, though his hair had gone white at the temples. A doctoral candidate’s blue cord hung frayed around his neck.

On the wall before him, someone had drawn a crooked doorway in charcoal.

The drawing opened.

Not physically. The stone remained stone, but the air folded inward, revealing a black depth beyond the marks. Something on the other side breathed.

“Don’t,” Eli said.

Kael’s fingers twitched. The doorway vanished.

“You saw it,” Kael said.

“Saw what?”

“The brace.”

Kael’s voice was dry from disuse. His eyes lifted, pale and fever-bright. Tiny lines of light crossed his irises like diagrams.

“Everything has braces,” he said. “Spells, buildings, arguments. They hold the shape in place. If you see them, you can tell what a thing is carrying.”

“And if you can’t?”

“You become a staircase.”

Eli crouched several feet away. The codex beneath his shirt warmed against his ribs.

“I need to know about the Foundational Texts.”

Kael laughed once, without amusement. “Everyone needs to know about the Foundational Texts. That’s why they’re foundational.”

“Wren says they were made from older knowledge.”

“Wren is right.”

The answer came so quickly Eli forgot to breathe.

Kael leaned his head against the wall. “The Principles of Matter are not principles. They’re commands. The Axioms of Rhetoric are permissions written in the grammar of certainty. The Canon of Healing was taken from midwives, bone-setters, apothecaries, and plague workers, then rewritten so the methods obey the seal of a degree.”

“Why does that matter?”

“Because commands can be revoked.”

The lines in Kael’s eyes shifted. For an instant Eli saw the ward differently: a lattice beneath the walls, symbols tied into the university’s foundations. The door was held shut by three red strokes. The nurse’s token had a knot of authority in its center. Even Eli’s body was outlined by trembling braces.

At his chest, the codex appeared as a blank space in the lattice.

Kael stared at it. “You have one.”

“A book?”

“A refusal.”

Kael reached for a shard of slate. “They broke me during the Trials. My Discipline was textual reconstruction. I could find what had been removed from a passage, what a sentence was hiding. They made me read the First Law until I could see its framework.”

“What happened?”

“I saw the first lie.”

His hand shook.

“They weren’t laws of the world. They were locks. Someone wrote, ‘Only the accredited may command,’ and built every later sentence around it. Repetition made the agreement heavy. Degrees made it portable.”

Eli thought of Wren treating the injured protester with old names while licensed healers watched.

“Can you undo it?”

“Not by arguing with the command. You name what the command was placed over.”

Kael drew a small circle on the floor. Inside it he wrote an angular mark. The mark flared, and a brass graduate assistant’s badge appeared in his palm.

“This claims mastery over citation,” he said. “It commands words to point toward authority.”

He closed his eyes. “Paper.”

Nothing happened. His face tightened.

“Not the sanctioned name,” he whispered. “The true one.”

Eli listened. Pipes muttered in the walls. A drain struggled beneath the floor. Beneath the badge’s enchantment he sensed a brittle scrape, like a page dragged over stone.

“Borrowed voice,” Eli said.

The badge went dark.

Its silver emblem flaked away. The brass softened, sagged, and dropped from Kael’s hand as an ordinary piece of stamped metal.

Eli stared at it.

“It isn’t enough to know the command,” Kael said. “You must know what it concealed.”

“Then help us.”

“Us?”

“People who are done asking permission.”

Kael studied him. “You want a weapon.”

“I want a way to keep people from being helpless.”

“That is a more dangerous weapon.”

He stood. His knees buckled, and Eli caught his arm. Beneath Kael’s skin, the scaffolding of his body flashed into view: fractured braces, missing supports, a black Discipline wound threaded through his spine.

“Don’t mistake standing for healing,” Kael said.

“I won’t.”

At the ward entrance, the nurse rose in alarm. “He cannot leave.”

Kael looked at her. The lines in his eyes brightened.

“Can’t,” he said, “is usually a command.”

The nurse’s mouth opened, then closed.

Eli guided him toward the lift. Behind them, the charcoal doorway remained crooked on the wall, waiting.

At the lift, Kael stopped and looked upward, toward the city of towers, bells, degrees, and locked doors.

“Tell Wren I remember the first name.”

“Which one?”

Kael’s broken smile held no comfort.

“The name before permission.”

Then he stepped into the lift beside Eli, and together they began to rise.

chapters.title: The Commons Converge
chapters.text:
The steam tunnels beneath Veritas had never been designed for meetings. They carried heat from the furnaces to dormitories, lecture halls, infirmaries, and towers above. Pipes crossed overhead in sweating bundles. The air tasted of iron and boiled stone.

But no professor owned them.

Eli entered through a service hatch with Kael leaning against his shoulder. Behind them came two expelled students, three of Wren’s apprentices, and Mira, an adjunct Rhetorics lecturer dismissed that afternoon for “unauthorized interpretive sympathy.” She carried her papers in a leather satchel and wore one shoe.

“You said there would be thirty,” she told Eli.

“There may be thirty.”

“There are eleven.”

“The others may be late.”

Dax, broad-shouldered and blackened to the elbows from the forge, stood beside a pressure valve. A hammer hung at his belt. Someone had scored a line through the university seal painted on the brass wheel.

More people arrived in twos and threes: a lift mechanic from the southern wards, an old mason with a sack of tools, two kitchen workers, a boy with ink-burned fingertips, and several adjuncts who looked as if they had come directly from being frightened.

They gathered beneath the largest pipe, where the ceiling rose high enough to stand upright. Someone had chalked the three-crossed-circle symbol onto the wall.

Kael stared at it.

“Do you know that mark?” Eli asked.

“I know it was covered.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“It is, to a scholar.”

Dax heard him. “We don’t need scholars.”

Mira turned. “You need people who know how to make a city listen.”

“We need people who know how to make a city burn.”

The gathering fell quiet.

Dax stepped forward. “They doubled tuition. Cut meals. Threw students into the street for speaking during a lecture. They burned guild workshops because old women knew how to fix pipes without kneeling to a professor. And you want to make the city listen?”

“I want the city to survive,” Mira said.

“Survival is what they call obedience when they’re hungry.”

A murmur moved through the tunnel. Eli felt the group pulling apart, like pressure gathering behind a flawed seam.

Mira set her satchel on a crate. “The university is rotten, yes. But it is also the infirmary, the libraries, the waterworks, the archives. Destroy it and you destroy the people who depend on it. Reform is possible. We can demand open examinations, adjunct representation, restored meals, and recognition for practical disciplines.”

“Recognition,” Dax said. “You still want them to put a seal on us.”

“I want protection.”

“You want permission.”

Mira flinched.

Eli looked at the gathered faces: tired, wary, and bright with the dangerous hope that came before courage or disaster. He thought of Kael in the ward, and of Wren’s warning that names let people work without permission.

“We’re arguing about whether to ask the lock to open,” he said, “or smash the door.”

Dax’s hand tightened around his hammer.

“Neither,” Eli continued. “We show everyone the door was never locked by nature.”

No one spoke.

Eli drew the blank codex from inside his coat. Its pale cover seemed to drain color from the tunnel.

“The university says its power comes from truth,” he said. “It doesn’t. It comes from commands repeated until everyone forgets they were commands. Only the accredited may command. Only the examined may heal. Only the cited may speak. These are not laws of the world. They are permissions someone wrote down and taught us to fear.”

Mira studied him. “What replaces them?”

“What we already have.”

The lift mechanic raised a hand. “We don’t have degrees.”

“No,” Eli said. “You have hands. You know which cables sing before they snap. You know how to draw heat from a cracked boiler. You know which herbs stop a fever and which ones kill. None of that becomes true when a professor stamps it.”

“Knowledge without standards becomes chaos,” said one adjunct.

“Then make standards together. Write them where everyone can read them. Teach them openly. Correct one another. Let no one turn understanding into a locked room.”

Dax gave a humorless laugh. “And when the proctors come?”

A blue light flickered at the far end of the tunnel.

A graduate assistant stepped through the hatch, robes immaculate despite the soot, a citation badge shining at his throat. He was young, but wore authority like armor.

“By decree of the Chancellor,” he announced, “this unauthorized assembly is dissolved. All present will identify themselves for disciplinary review.”

The badge pulsed.

“You will listen,” he said.

Several people lowered their eyes.

Kael moved first. He crossed the tunnel with a stiff, uneven gait. Eli reached for him, but Kael shook his head. His gaze fixed on something beneath the assistant’s robes.

“Do you know what it says?” Kael asked.

“I know what it commands.”

“No. You know what it repeats.”

The badge flashed.

Kael lifted a trembling finger. “Citation. Authority. Direction. Borrowed voice.”

Black lines appeared beneath the skin of his neck, ink leaking through paper. Eli saw the braces around his body, fractured and overstrained.

“Kael,” he warned.

“Name what it hides,” Kael whispered.

Eli looked at the badge. It did not contain authority. It contained the demand to be mistaken for authority.

“Borrowed voice,” Eli said.

The badge went dull.

Its silver emblem sagged, softened, and slid down the assistant’s robe as a lump of ordinary metal. The blue light vanished. The words in the tunnel straightened.

The assistant stared at the ruined clasp.

Dax drew his hammer.

“Don’t,” Eli said.

The hammer stopped.

The graduate assistant backed toward the hatch, suddenly only a frightened young man in a fine robe. No one touched him. He fled anyway.

For several heartbeats, the only sound was steam moving through the pipes.

Then the old mason laughed. The kitchen workers joined him. One expelled student covered her mouth. Mira looked from Kael to the dead badge.

“You didn’t destroy it,” she said.

Kael swayed. Eli caught him.

“No,” Kael murmured. “We told it what it was.”

The words passed through the assembly.

Not destroy. Name.

The mechanic stepped toward the chalked symbol and laid her palm over its three crossed lines. “My mother knew the old pressure songs. The university called them superstition.”

“My grandfather built bridges without a degree,” said the mason. “They took his measurements and published them under a professor’s name.”

The boy with ink-blackened fingers lifted his chin. “I can read three dead languages. The registrar says it’s worthless because I learned them from a sewer archivist.”

Dax looked around at them, his hammer lowered.

“So what?” he asked. “We make a club?”

“We make a commons,” Eli said.

The word seemed larger than the tunnel.

Mira opened her satchel and set her lecture notes on the crate. “I know the traps in sanctioned rhetoric—the ways a sentence makes obedience sound inevitable.”

Dax glanced at the papers. “I know fire. And metal. And how not to burn the people standing beside me.”

One by one, the others offered what they knew.

The pipes hissed overhead, carrying heat toward a city that had never thanked them. Beneath the university, among brick and steam, the gathered people began to speak their knowledge aloud—not as applicants or supplicants, but as heirs returning to an inheritance that had been stolen and renamed.

Eli listened.

For the first time, the tunnel did not sound like a hiding place.

It sounded like the beginning of an answer.

chapters.title: Blood and Tuition
chapters.text:
By morning, Decree Nine had been nailed to every door in Veritas.

Mira read it aloud in Wren’s workshop while the others crowded around the stove.

“‘All persons without recognized degree or guild license must register with the Office of Academic Belonging within three days. Failure to register constitutes outlawry. The teaching, practice, or circulation of unlicensed knowledge is hereby classified as heresy.’”

Dax snatched the decree from her. “They’ve called maintenance heresy?”

“They’ve called us heretics,” Mira said.

Kael studied the page. His eyes moved across the letters without resting. “The seal is reinforced. The words are meant to enter the reader.”

Eli felt the command beneath the sentences, cold and patient.

Only the accredited may remain.

Wren folded the decree and fed it into the stove. The flames turned blue. For one breath, everyone lowered their eyes.

Then Wren struck the stove with her tongs.

“Look up.”

They did.

The raids began before noon.

Proctors descended into the Undercroft in lacquered armor, graduate assistants behind them carrying citation rods and bundles of white paper constructs. The first guild workshop burned beneath the old baths. Annotated oil soaked the benches and burned hotter whenever someone tried to smother it.

At the next, the proctors tore apart looms and arrested anyone who could not produce a registration token. At the third, a professor of Applied Ethics declared the eviction “a pedagogically essential correction.”

Smoke rolled through the lower streets.

A runner reached Wren’s workshop, soot-blackened and gasping. “They’re coming here.”

“Back tunnel,” Wren ordered. “Everyone who can walk, walk. Everyone who cannot, is carried.”

The workshop emptied into the old maintenance passage. Its only open exit ended at a massive steam gate beneath Foundry Road, an iron door designed to contain pressure from the city’s oldest mains.

Eli crouched beside the mechanism. The locking wheel shuddered under his hands.

“Vey,” he said. “Pressure seeking release.”

“Orn,” Wren answered. “The left hinge is holding it.”

A blast struck the other side. Steam shrieked through the seams.

Kael stared at the door. Black lines showed beneath the skin of his throat, the hidden braces of his body tightening. “Its command is broken,” he said. “It says hold, but the hinges no longer mean hold.”

“Can you unwrite it?” Mira asked.

“Not while it is holding us and the city.”

Another impact shook the passage.

Dax shoved open the inner gate. “Move!”

Wren seized Eli by the collar as he reached for the wheel again.

“Go.”

“I can fix it.”

“You can open it. You cannot make iron young.”

She placed her tongs in his hands.

“Take the names,” she said.

Blue fire splashed across the workshop behind them. A paper construct crawled over the ceiling, its seal-face opening like a mouth.

Wren stepped between it and the gate.

“Wren!”

She looked back once. Her face was lit by fire and steam, older than the city and steadier than stone.

“Kes,” she called.

The word passed through the chamber: the quiet before a pipe bursts, the instant in which a choice remains possible.

Then Wren drove her shoulder into the wheel.

Eli dragged Kael through the passage. Mira followed, shouting for the others to keep moving. Behind them, the gate groaned.

“Vey!” Wren cried.

The wheel turned.

“Orn!”

The iron screamed.

Eli looked back. Wren stood in the narrowing opening, both hands locked around the wheel, steam lifting her hair. A citation rod flashed in the workshop.

The gate slammed shut.

They stumbled through the drainage galleries until the smoke thinned. No one spoke. Behind the wall, the main gave one enormous exhalation.

Then silence.

Dax struck the stone with both fists. “We left her.”

“She made us leave,” Mira said.

“She made herself stay.”

Eli still held the tongs. Their handles had blistered his palms. Kael gently pulled them away.

They emerged at dusk beneath an abandoned cistern. The survivors counted themselves in the rain.

Wren was not among them.

They found her body in the square outside the old guildhall.

The proctors had bound her upright to a maintenance post, her hands fixed around a broken wrench. A sheet of parchment covered her chest.

CITED FOR HERESY: WREN, FORMER MASTER OF LOWER MAINTENANCE.

Beneath it were the charges: unauthorized instruction, obstruction of lawful scholarship, conspiracy against accredited order.

Dax reached for his hammer.

Eli stopped him.

Wren’s hands remained visible beneath the parchment. The fingers were blackened, the nails split, but they held the wrench as though she were still repairing something.

Kael stared at the sheet. “They’ve made her into an argument.”

“No,” Eli said.

He tore the parchment down.

The paper writhed, trying to name itself law. Eli looked at Wren, at the wrench, and at the people gathering in the rain.

“Her name was Wren,” he said. “She knew vey. She knew orn. She knew kes. She knew how stone fails, how pressure lies, how a frightened child breathes. She taught without permission because permission was never required for truth.”

The parchment went still.

“This is not a citation,” Eli said. “It is borrowed voice.”

The letters faded.

Around the square, people began speaking. Names for hinges, fever, mortar, grain, river current, smoke—names the university had buried beneath seals and fees.

Eli laid the dead parchment over Wren’s feet.

“Take her down.”

Together, they cut the ropes.

That night, beneath the guildhall, they lit no funeral pyre. Fire was too easy to claim as evidence. Instead they gathered around Wren’s tools and spoke until dawn, each person adding a true name to the inheritance.

Eli stood at the center, the blank codex beneath his coat.

“When we go to the Chancellor,” he said, “we will not beg him to recognize us.”

His voice shook, but did not break.

“We will carry Wren’s names to his door. And we will ask him what, exactly, gives him the right to close it.”

chapters.title: The Lexicon Foundry
chapters.text:
The Lexicon Foundry stood between the old law courts and the river, a fortress of black brick threaded with copper pipes. Its chimneys breathed white vapor over the rooftops. Every breath smelled of burnt sugar, hot metal, and sweat.

For three days, the Commons had watched it.

Students entered through the eastern gate wearing gray labor collars. They emerged hours later with trembling hands and empty eyes. Between those passages, the Foundry took what the university called *cognitive surplus*—attention, memory, invention—and distilled it into degree ink.

At dawn, its bell rang once.

Dax tightened his grip on an iron pry bar. “That’s our bell.”

“It’s their bell,” Mira said. “We’re borrowing it.”

“Borrowed voice,” Eli murmured.

The phrase had become their signal. Not a slogan. A diagnosis.

Thirty volunteers crouched in the drainage culvert behind them. Wren’s apprentices carried hammers; expelled students carried stolen citation rods; two kitchen workers bore sacks of flour to blind the proctor-spiders. Mira held a ring of copied keys.

Kael stood beside Eli, braced against the wall. His face was gray. The black wound threaded through his spine pulsed whenever the university’s wards stirred.

“You should stay here,” Eli said.

Kael gave him a thin smile. “I am staying here. Until the Foundry is inside me.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

“It wasn’t intended to be.”

The eastern gate opened for a coal cart. Dax threw the first flour sack.

White powder burst across the gatehouse. Guards shouted. One proctor raised a citation rod, but Mira spoke three quick syllables, shaping them into a sentence that left no room for interruption.

“Your authority is presently under review.”

The rod flickered. Its blue flame died.

The Commons surged.

Eli ran beneath the gate and into the central hall. Pipes crossed overhead like the ribs of a buried animal. Along the walls, brass cylinders churned with cloudy gold fluid. Scraps of paper, hair, fingernails, and fragments of handwriting floated inside—pieces of students rendered into ink.

The Press of Words occupied the far end of the hall. It was taller than a chapel, built from ironwood and silver gears. A blank parchment slid beneath its descending head. Each strike produced a degree: Bachelor of Principles, Master of Applied Rhetoric, Doctor of Licensed Matter.

Around it, indentured students fed the machine.

Some were no older than sixteen.

“Stop the press!” Dax roared.

The workers looked up. A shaved-headed boy shook his chains. “We can’t!”

“You can,” Eli said.

He saw the mechanism as Wren would have seen it: not a spell, but a pressure system. The press inhaled before every strike. A vey gathered in the upper chamber, seeking release. Below, the left brace trembled.

“When it rises, move!” Eli shouted.

A graduate assistant appeared on the catwalk, robes snapping around his ankles. His silver badge gleamed.

“By Decree Nine,” he called, “all unauthorized persons are subject to—”

Kael lifted one hand.

The badge split down the center.

Silver peeled from brass. The university seal became a circle, then a smear, then nothing. The assistant stared at his bare coat. Dax climbed the stairs and struck him with the pry bar.

The press descended.

Eli thrust Wren’s tongs into the upper chamber.

“Vey,” he said.

The machine screamed. Steam burst from its joints. The press halted an inch above the parchment, shuddering with trapped force.

Eli turned toward the left brace.

“Orn,” he said. “Pressure trapped by a flaw in your vessel.”

The brace split.

Every gear in the Foundry lurched.

Mira and the kitchen workers broke the students’ chains while rebels fought the guards. Some freed students stumbled away, unable to stand after months of harvested thought. Others seized hammers and joined the attack.

A rack of blank degrees toppled near Kael.

The parchments were not empty. They were waiting, each one a mouth without a voice. Kael touched the first sheet.

His body convulsed.

“What do you see?” Eli asked.

“The permission,” Kael gasped. “Under the fibers.”

He moved from parchment to parchment, fingers leaving dark smudges. The blank degrees curled inward and turned gray.

“Only the accredited may command,” the parchments whispered.

Kael pressed both hands against the rack.

“No,” he said. “Only the commanded must obey.”

The rack exploded.

Parchment filled the air like dead birds. The chimneys belched black smoke. Somewhere below, a pressure vessel burst, and the floor heaved.

Then the Citation Elemental came through the smoke.

It had once been a legal paragraph. Now it wore a body of burning quotations, each sentence chained to the next in red ink. Its head was a sealed citation mark. Its hands ended in sharpened brackets.

“Unauthorized source,” it said.

One bracket struck Dax and hurled him into a vat.

The other went for Eli.

Kael stepped between them.

The bracket entered his side.

For a moment there was no sound. Then Kael screamed, and every letter in the elemental’s body blazed white.

Eli caught him as his knees folded. Blood ran black between Eli’s fingers.

“Go,” Kael said.

“No.”

“The Foundry is collapsing.”

The main pipes had begun to buckle. Freed students poured toward the eastern gate, carrying friends and armfuls of blank parchment. Three rebels lay beneath the fallen catwalk. Others were dragged away by proctors arriving through the smoke.

Mira seized Eli’s shoulder. “We have to leave now.”

The elemental turned toward them.

Eli looked at Wren’s tongs, at Kael’s blood, at the press straining against its jammed command.

He remembered Wren’s voice: *You can open it. You cannot make old iron young.*

“Kes,” Eli said.

The instant held.

He drove the tongs into the press’s fracture.

The machine released its pressure all at once.

Steam tore through the hall. The elemental shattered into strips of burning paper. The press split from crown to base, and the Foundry’s great windows burst outward over the river.

Eli, Mira, and Dax dragged Kael through the gate as the roof collapsed behind them.

They made it three streets before the bells began.

Not the Foundry’s bell. Every bell in Veritas.

Citizens emerged onto rooftops. Workers stopped along the bridges and turned toward the black plume rising over the river. A parchment degree struck a statue’s face and slid down its stone cheek, blank and harmless.

The university had lost a machine.

The city had seen it bleed.

Behind them, proctors captured seven rebels. Ahead, Kael’s blood darkened the stones.

Eli held Wren’s tongs in one hand and Kael’s wrist in the other.

“Keep moving,” Mira said.

So they did, beneath the ringing bells, while all across Veritas people began asking what else could be broken.

chapters.title: The Ivory Ward Falls
chapters.text:
By noon, the Lexicon Foundry’s smoke had spread across half the sky.

Beneath it, in a disused tram depot, the Commons counted their losses. Seven captured. Three missing. More injured than they had clean cloth for.

Kael lay on a door used as a stretcher. A kitchen worker named Sella kept pressure on his wound while he stared past her shoulder.

“He needs beds, water, somewhere clean,” she said. “Not another tunnel.”

Mira unfolded a map on the floor. It bore the ivory-and-blue seal of her old department.

“The Ward of Rhetorics has all three.”

Dax looked up. “And professors.”

“Most of its guards went to the Foundry. By morning they’ll return.”

Eli crouched beside her. The map showed lecture halls, private staircases, a central auditorium. Under the blue corridors, faint dotted lines marked an older building.

“What’s underneath?”

“Cisterns. Supposedly filled when the Ward expanded.”

He traced a line connecting them to the kitchens. “Covered, not filled. They still need ventilation.”

Mira met his eyes. “A way in?”

“And a way to make staying inside unpleasant.”

They left at dusk.

Mechanics entered through a laundry conduit. Mira led expelled students toward the public gates. Dax drove a cart beneath a stolen hygiene-department canvas, with Kael and the wounded concealed inside.

Eli walked beside the wheel. Wren’s tongs knocked against his thigh.

The Ivory Ward rose above the street in pale stone and blue glass. Over its doors, gold letters proclaimed: **REASON ADMITS ALL WHO ARE WORTHY.**

Two graduate assistants guarded the gate.

“Department?” one demanded.
