Vance tested the restraints. They tightened in response.

“What are you going to do?”

“You have already read the answer,” said Surgeon Vey.

He emerged from behind the slab. The puncture beneath Vance’s jaw still burned.

“Do not distress him before the address,” said Archivist Seraphine.

She sat in a chair made from fused vertebrae. Silver filaments hung from her shaved scalp and disappeared into its upholstery. Beside her rested a cylinder of black fluid. Something pale moved within it.

Malkus came close. He smelled of antiseptic, damp soil, and old meat.

“Elias Vance,” he said. “Legacy Candidate Zero-One. Neurologist. Architect of suspended cognition. The most stable mind to emerge from the old world.”

“I didn’t architect this.”

“No,” Seraphine said. “You merely helped make it possible.”

Memory stirred: fluorescent rooms, a patient’s scalp beneath a ring of electrodes, his own voice explaining that consciousness might be patterned without being preserved. Then illness. A consent form. A blank interval.

Malkus raised one clawed hand. The clicking in the galleries stopped.

“For one thousand and twelve years, the Faculty maintained this station and its mission. We endured atmospheric collapse, famine, war, fungal invasion, and the failure of every surface refuge. We altered ourselves because nature had become an adversary. Chitin for protection. Auxiliary exchange organs for poisoned air. Efficient metabolisms for scarcity.”

A low chant began beneath the theater. It moved through the floor, too deep to be machinery. Vance felt it in his teeth.

“Our adaptations are failing,” Malkus continued. “Cellular repair loops have accumulated errors. Neural matrices decay. The archives preserve memory, but memory is not renewal. We require a cognitive substrate untouched by a millennium of correction.”

“An unmutated mind,” Vance said.

“An intact one,” Seraphine corrected. “You are not merely unmutated. You are curated. Hormonal modulation. Microchimeric reinforcement. Synaptic conditioning. Every alteration brought you closer to this moment.”

The words entered him with surgical precision. They had changed him while he slept, turning his body into an instrument and calling the process preservation.

“What moment?”

“The Sublimation.”

A monitor beside his head lit. An image unfolded above it: a silver mesh descending through a human brain and converging in a black, pulsing mass.

“We will lace your cortex,” Malkus said. “Your neural architecture will be transferred through the Faculty Continuity Protocol. The viable portions of your cognition will replenish our failing intelligences. Your memories and adaptive capacity will be distributed among us.”

“And my body?”

Seraphine’s expression softened.

“Your body will nourish the station.”

Vance pulled against the restraints until pain flashed behind his eyes.

“You call that medicine?”

“The ultimate medical sacrifice,” she said. “One life, freely preserved, sustaining a civilization.”

“I did not consent.”

“Consent is a primitive model,” Malkus replied. “You consented when you entered preservation.”

“I consented to treatment.”

“You consented to continuation.”

The distinction was clean and merciless.

At the edge of the theater, Imago shifted.

“Provost,” he said.

Malkus turned. “Yes?”

Imago’s hands tightened. “The procedure constitutes—”

“Constitutes what?”

Imago looked toward Vance. His compound eyes reflected the restraints in dozens of tiny lights.

“Constitutes murder,” he said.

The theater went still.

Vey hissed through his teeth. Seraphine’s fingers curled over her chair.

Malkus approached Imago until their faces were level.

“You object to continuity?”

“I object to—”

“You object to the use of a resource entrusted to us?”

Imago lowered his gaze.

“You have eaten from the same bodies you now claim to defend,” Malkus said. “You restrained the resistant, sedated the unstable, and prepared the dead. Do not discover ethics only because this specimen resembles you.”

Imago flinched.

For an instant, shame made him seem more human than any unaltered face Vance had seen in the station.

Malkus turned back to the slab.

“The Sublimation begins at second bell.”

“When is that?”

“Three hours.”

The word became an interval. A window.

Malkus lifted his hand. The apparatus above Vance unfolded, needles descending to test the air.

“Rest,” said Seraphine. “Fear consumes cognitive yield.”

The Faculty withdrew through the galleries. Vey followed. Imago remained until the doors had sealed.

“I am sorry,” he whispered.

Vance watched him. “Are you?”

Imago’s mouth opened, exposing small inner teeth. “I do not know what I am.”

Then he turned away, and the door closed behind him.

Vance lay beneath the instruments while the chant rose through the floor.

He had spent his life studying failure: the misfiring neuron, the infected cell, the body turning against itself. Disease was not evil. It was strategy without conscience, replication without permission. It entered through weakness, learned its host, and used every system designed to preserve life.

The Faculty believed he was a patient because they had placed him on a table.

They believed he was a resource because they had named him one.

They believed his mind would remain orderly until they opened it.

Vance stopped pulling against the restraints. Pain was data. Panic was metabolic waste. The slab had sensors. The room had cameras. Somewhere below, the Pattern—or whatever fed the chant—was listening.

He closed his eyes and inventoried the theater.

Six visible exits. Three active monitors. Two restraint circuits. One anesthetic line. Imago’s hesitation. Malkus’s impatience. Seraphine’s dependence on procedure. Vey’s confidence.

The apparatus descended another centimeter.

Vance breathed slowly through his nose.

If they intended to preserve him, he would become contamination. If they intended to copy him, he would become noise. If they intended to digest his mind, he would give them something that could not be digested.

For the first time since waking, fear became useful.

He began, silently, to design the disease.

chapters.title: Obolus's Testament
chapters.text:
The cell had no door, only a translucent membrane stretched across the opening. It contracted with the station’s breathing, drawing in damp air that smelled of fungus, antiseptic, and the sweet iron reek of processing rooms.

Vance sat on the cot, wrists marked by restraints. Somewhere beyond the walls, machinery counted toward the second bell.

He had tried to reconstruct his life and found only fragments: a lecture hall, a woman’s hand on his shoulder, a consent form glowing on glass, the sensation of drowning in cold. Then darkness, edited into a single breath.

The membrane rippled.

An old creature entered carrying a metal case. Its carapace was split along the chest and abdomen, held together by black sutures and medical tape. Clear fluid leaked from the seams. Beneath the broken shell, pale fibers trembled with every breath.

“You are Elias Vance,” it said.

Its voice rasped like an ancient recording.

“I was.”

The creature tilted its head. Clouded eyes nestled beneath layered chitin; sensory filaments curled along its cheeks.

“Good. You still distinguish the past from the present.”

“Who are you?”

“Curator Obolus.”

“A coin placed in the mouth of the dead.”

“A suitable name for an institution that has forgotten the value of the living.”

Obolus lowered itself to the floor. Its shell cracked again.

Vance watched fluid gather beneath it. “You’re dying.”

“We are all dying. I am merely less successful at disguising it.”

The curator opened the case. Inside lay a black keycard and a narrow glass vial filled with amber liquid. A filament of something darker drifted within, curling like a drowned larva.

“What is that?”

“The keycard opens a maintenance route below the Recovery Ward. The vial is older than Malkus, perhaps older than the station’s first lies.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No. It is a warning.”

Obolus lifted the vial. “Before controlled mutation, there were wild adaptive strains. Unstable. Most killed their hosts. A few remade them.”

“You want me to inject myself with it?”

“I want you to understand why the Sublimation will work.”

Vance stood. “They said I was unmutated.”

“They said what made the harvest convenient.”

The old creature’s voice softened. “You have not been pure for centuries.”

The words struck harder than Vey’s needle.

“Explain.”

“During preservation, your endocrine system was adjusted to slow decay and improve cellular compliance. Your neural responses were conditioned for patterned interfaces. Microchimeric cells from other donors were seeded into your marrow and nervous system. Your immune system was softened, then trained again.”

“I was in cryostasis.”

“Cryostasis is not stillness here. You were opened, sampled, repaired, and sealed again. Sometimes decades passed between interventions. Sometimes centuries.”

Vance looked at his hands. They were still his: long fingers, blunt nails, the scar at the base of his thumb from a surgical blade slipping during residency.

“The scars.”

“Access points.”

“The dreams?”

“Neural conditioning.”

“The gaps in my memory?”

Obolus did not answer.

Cold spread through Vance, unrelated to the chamber. “Did I consent to this?”

“You consented to treatment.”

“That is not what I asked.”

“No,” Obolus said. “It is not.”

The chant from below rose through the walls, a single syllable carried by many voices. Vance had thought it prayer. Now it sounded like a machine learning to speak.

“I built Palingenesis,” he said. “Or part of it.”

“You designed the suspension architecture.”

“For patients who could not be cured in their own time.”

“For patients who could be useful in ours.”

“I would never have agreed to that.”

“Would you have agreed to save a civilization?”

“I would have agreed to save people.”

Obolus gave a dry click. “That distinction was the first thing we lost.”

Vance stared at the vial. The dark filament inside moved against the glass, tracing slow loops as though it sensed him.

“I wrote the ethical standards for Palingenesis,” Obolus continued. “I argued that no patient could be reduced to future utility. I swore an oath to protect the vulnerable from those who called necessity a virtue.”

“And then?”

“The sky failed. Crops failed. The refuges failed. Children starved beneath clean-room lights while our colleagues calculated caloric yield from the dead.” Obolus touched the split in its chest. “We told ourselves survival would be temporary. Every compromise became a precedent. Every precedent became law.”

“You became the Faculty.”

“We became what the law was designed to prevent.”

Obolus pushed the vial across the cot. “The strain does not obey the Faculty’s controls. It adapts according to stress, environment, and whatever remains buried in the host. If you take it, you may become something they cannot digest.”

“Or it may kill me.”

“Yes.”

Vance almost laughed. “You offer terrible alternatives.”

“I offer an honest one.”

He picked up the vial. It was warm.

“Why tell me this?” he asked.

“Because your body is not merely altered. It was tuned. Hormonal cycles, neural conditioning, donor cells—each intervention prepared you for their harvest. You are a tool shaped to fit their machine.”

His reflection trembled in the amber liquid: a gaunt face, silver hair, eyes belonging to a man who had lost a thousand years without living them.

“Then what’s left of me?”

Obolus leaned forward, fluid dripping from its carapace.

“They changed your body. They buried your choices beneath procedure. But a tool does not ask whether it is a tool.”

The answer did not restore Vance’s humanity. It only gave his horror a direction.

“What do you want from me?”

“Destroy the Pattern.”

“The black mass.”

“The archive, the engine, the appetite. Every mind they consumed is in it, or near it, or screaming through it. The Faculty calls that continuity. It is only accumulation.”

“And you?”

“I am already in its shadow.”

Obolus reached for the keycard, then stopped. “Take it.”

Vance did.

At the membrane, the curator paused. A wet crack traveled through its shell.

“Why help me now?”

For the first time, Obolus looked directly at him.

“Because I remember the oath,” it whispered. “And because I am tired of surviving what I became.”

The membrane opened. Obolus disappeared into the fungal dark, leaving a thin trail of luminous fluid behind.

Vance stood alone with the keycard in one hand and the vial in the other.

The chant deepened. The station seemed to recognize his choice before he made it.

He closed his fingers around the strain.

“Destroy the Pattern,” Obolus had said.

Then, almost too softly to hear:

“Let me die.”

chapters.title: The Extraction
chapters.text:
The cell opened without an alarm.

Vance held Obolus’s card against the plate beside the membrane. The translucent seal slackened, peeling away with a wet sound. Beyond it, the corridor was empty except for the luminous drops the Curator had left behind.

He followed them until they turned toward the lifts. Then he went the other way.

The vial knocked against his ribs inside his borrowed gown. He cupped it through the cloth, afraid of breaking it, more afraid of what would make him choose to open it.

Beneath the Recovery Ward, the keycard admitted him to a maintenance recess. A ventilation grille hung crookedly above a bank of dead monitors. He climbed the console and pulled himself into the opening.

The duct was warm and furred with pale growth. Every movement sent pain through his shoulders. Somewhere below, someone coughed, then began the same cough again, with precisely the same catch of breath.

A recording, he told himself.

He crawled faster.

The chant thickened as the duct descended. Through its metal floor he felt machinery gathering speed. At the next junction, blue light shone through a grille.

He lowered his face.

Mira lay in a cradle beneath a ring of surgical lamps.

Her wheelchair stood beside the wall, one footplate folded up. That ordinary little asymmetry almost undid him. Her wrists were secured, her head enclosed in a delicate silver framework. Filaments descended from it into needles along her scalp and neck. Beneath the transparent cradle, cables hung like roots.

Vey stood at her shoulder.

“Reference cognition remains coherent,” the Surgeon said.

Seraphine watched a display. “Increase acquisition. We require a stable calibration before Zero-One arrives.”

They were testing the apparatus on her.

Vance pressed his mouth against his wrist.

Mira’s lips moved. He could not hear her over the machinery, but he recognized the shape of a word.

Please.

Then light rose through the floor.

What he had taken for dark glass beneath the cradle became transparent, revealing something vast in the chamber below. Pale folds swelled against retaining ribs. Black fluid moved through channels between them. Silver threads converged in knots that brightened and dimmed, and with each pulse the mass contracted.

There were shapes embedded in it that resembled faces only until he tried to look directly at them.

The Pattern.

Obolus had called it an appetite. Vance had imagined a machine with a biological component. This thing filled the foundations.

Mira cried out.

Her voice came again a moment later from beneath the floor.

Vance pulled back from the grille.

A service panel occupied the duct wall. Its faded diagram meant little to him, but he recognized the warning strip marking an emergency power transfer. Beside it, through a second opening, he could see a recessed control station below.

He eased the grille inward and dropped behind a column of insulated pipes. Pain flared through his ankles. Neither Vey nor Seraphine turned.

The keycard woke the station.

A maintenance screen offered him a choice between isolating the chamber and transferring its load. He selected transfer. A warning bloomed across the display: the receiving system was unavailable.

He confirmed anyway.

For one breath, nothing happened.

Then the lamps burned white.

A crack snapped overhead. Seraphine staggered from her console as sparks scattered across it. The chant broke into separate voices, abruptly frightened.

Vance ran toward the cradle.

At its base, a red lever sat beneath a shield marked CENTRAL LACE ISOLATION. Through the glass below, the converging silver threads blazed. If that lever severed the feed, perhaps the surge would finish what he had begun.

He reached for it.

Mira’s body arched against the restraints. A needle shifted at her throat, drawing a thin red line.

“Help me,” she said.

He turned away from the lever.

Vey came around the cradle. “You will destroy the reference.”

Vance caught the wheelchair by its handles and shoved it into the Surgeon’s legs. Vey fell against a console. The impact rang through the chamber.

There was no time to understand the release controls. Vance tore open the wrist straps, then found the catch beneath the silver framework. It resisted. Mira stared past him while the filaments trembled.

“Look at me,” he said. “Mira. It’s Elias.”

“The food,” she whispered.

“I know.”

“The food.”

He wrenched the catch upward.

The framework opened. Needles withdrew unevenly; one remained caught until he pulled it free with fingers already slippery with blood. He pressed a fold of his gown against her neck and lifted her.

She was terribly light.

Her eyes opened fully.

There was no recognition in them.

“Mira?”

“The food,” she said, in the exact cadence he remembered from the ward.

Beneath their feet, her voice said, “Please don’t let them.”

He nearly dropped her.

Seraphine was shouting into a wall receiver. Doors unfolded along the far side of the chamber, admitting low, chitinous bodies. Their jointed limbs struck the floor in a rapid clatter. Drones, some bearing instruments, others only hooked forelegs.

Vance backed toward the service exit.

Imago stood in it.

For an instant relief weakened Vance’s knees.

Then Imago extended one long arm across the doorway.

“Containment breach,” he said to the approaching drones. “The candidate must remain intact.”

“Move.”

“Put her down, Elias.”

Behind him, Vey was getting up.

Vance shifted Mira against his chest. Her head rolled onto his shoulder, eyes fixed on Imago.

“The food,” she told him.

Imago’s arm lowered an inch.

“She is experiencing residual speech,” he said.

“Look at her.”

“I can stabilize—”

“Look at her.”

One of the drones struck. A hook raked Vance’s upper arm, opening skin from shoulder to elbow. He stumbled into the doorframe. Mira made no sound.

Imago caught the drone’s limb.

“Intact,” he said sharply.

Vey shouted his name.

For a moment Imago held the creature back, staring at Mira’s face. His mouthparts moved without speech.

Then he shifted aside.

Vance pushed past him.

He ran badly, one arm failing beneath Mira’s weight, blood warming his wrist. Behind him came Vey’s voice and the clatter of pursuit. He followed the service passage downward, taking turns wherever the air felt cooler, until a heavy pump-room door yielded beneath his shoulder.

He dragged it shut and dropped the locking bar.

Only then did he lower Mira onto a bed of dry packing material beside the pipes.

Her pulse beat beneath his fingers. Her breathing continued. He checked both twice because they were the only answers he had.

Beyond the door, claws scraped metal.

Vance pressed his bleeding arm against his body and remembered Imago’s hand holding back the drone. Not forgiveness. Not even trust.

But he had moved aside.

In that small, dreadful hesitation, something had survived.

chapters.title: Mutation
chapters.text:
The pump room had been built to keep the station alive, and everything in it seemed to breathe.

Fungal mats pulsed along the walls. Pale caps opened over the pipes, releasing damp heat and the sour perfume of decay. Beneath the grating, a pump labored with the slow, uneven beat of an enormous heart.

Vance lowered Mira onto the floor between two conduits. Her head rolled toward him. The extraction needles had left pinpricks of blood along her throat, but her breathing remained steady. Her eyes stayed shut.

“Mira.”

Nothing.

Beyond the sealed door, metal scraped against metal. A drone clicked in the passage. Another answered.

“Dr. Vance,” Vey called through the door, his voice calm and amplified. “Your injuries require treatment. Open the door.”

Vance pressed his palm over the wound in his upper arm. Blood had soaked his sleeve. Pain was familiar, clean, and reassuring. The rest of him was not. His vision narrowed at the edges, and his heart raced in uneven bursts.

Mira’s mouth moved.

“The food.”

The words came in the same flat cadence as before, worn smooth by repetition. But beneath the floor, beneath the pumps and fungal roots, Vance could still hear her other voice.

Please don’t let them.

He reached inside his coat and drew out Obolus’s vial.

The black filament suspended in amber curled without any visible current. It looked less like a microorganism than a splinter of night. The label was handwritten and blurred with age.

Wild adaptive strain.

No dosage. No restrictions. Only the symbol Obolus had drawn beside it: a circle split by a jagged line.

Become something they cannot digest.

The door shuddered under a blow.

“Candidate Zero-One,” Vey said. “Your cognition is already compromised. Resistance will only damage the substrate.”

Vance thought of the records: the gentle voices, the food trays, the promise of rest. Everything had been arranged around the moment a living person became material.

He broke the seal.

The vial smelled of wet iron and opened graves.

For one second he considered pouring it down the drain. Then Mira made a small sound, almost a whimper, and the decision left him.

Vance drove the injector into his thigh and depressed the plunger.

The strain entered like ice.

He dropped the empty vial and caught himself against the wall. Something moved beneath his skin. His blood vessels darkened, branching upward from the injection site. Heat followed, boiling through his muscles.

His spine arched.

A crack sounded in his chest.

He fell beside Mira, fingers scraping at the floor. The fungal mat recoiled from his hand, then leaned toward him.

“No,” he said.

The word came out twice: once from his mouth, and once as a rasping answer from somewhere deeper.

His skin tightened across his forearms. Plates formed beneath it, pushing through in overlapping ridges. Chitin emerged ivory, then darkened to the color of old bone.

Vance screamed.

The sound struck the pipes and returned altered. Fungal bulbs contracted. Membranes trembled. Tiny pale insects poured from a valve and gathered in a spiral around him.

Pressure filled his skull.

Two pits opened beneath his cheekbones.

He felt the room through them.

Temperature became shape. Motion left trails. The drones beyond the door shone as clustered heat, their electrical hearts blinking in their torsos. The station unfolded into layers of living tissue, polymer, root, wire, and bone.

And threaded through everything was a chemical language.

Scent became grammar.

Fear was salt and copper. Pain was green bitterness. Obedience smelled of burned resin.

He smelled the Faculty through the door: Vey’s impatience, Seraphine’s cold attention, Malkus’s heavy command.

The new sense translated them into meanings that were not words.

Break. Open. Feed.

Vance pressed his hands to his head. “Stop.”

The walls answered with a pulse of intention.

Hatch. Hold. Consume. Become.

Insectoid grammar, he thought. Imperatives without the lies human language permitted.

Then the Pattern stirred below him.

Its pulse rose through the floor and entered his bones. Silver filaments flashed like nerves inside a body too large to comprehend. Fragments traveled with it: a child laughing; someone reciting a surgical oath; a woman begging for water; a man repeating his own name until it lost meaning.

Mira.

He knew her among the thousands.

Not whole. Not safe. A bright disturbance trapped inside the black current.

He reached for it.

The Pattern recoiled.

Every fungal mass in the room convulsed. The drones outside stopped scraping. For an instant, the entire facility held still.

Then the pulse changed.

It had noticed him.

Vance collapsed onto one elbow. His right hand had changed. The fingers were longer, the nails thickening into dark, translucent hooks. He flexed them, and the claws clicked against the floor.

He remembered those hands holding a scalpel.

He remembered designing the first suspension lattice, believing medicine could be made patient enough to outlast death.

He remembered his name.

Elias Vance.

The memories were incomplete, stained by other impressions, but they were his. He had been a doctor. He had not consented to this.

The conviction steadied him.

The door burst inward.

A drone thrust its head through the gap, mandibles opening. Vance saw the command current running through it. He smelled its directive.

Preserve the candidate.

It lunged.

Vance moved without deciding to move. His altered arm snapped forward. Claws punched through the drone’s throat assembly and pinned it against the frame. The machine convulsed, servos whining.

Hold, the new instinct whispered.

The drone’s heat faded beneath his grip.

He released it. The body collapsed. Behind it, the other drones hesitated.

Vance stared at his hand. Chitin had reached his wrist, ridged and glossy beneath the torn sleeve. Fine sensory hairs trembled along his knuckles, tasting the air.

Mira stirred.

Her eyelids fluttered, revealing only a dull gray sheen.

Vance lifted her carefully. Her head rested against his chest. Her pulse remained weak but regular.

“I’m here,” he said. “I’m still here.”

Her lips parted.

“The food.”

He looked down at her blank face and felt the Pattern pulsing below them, holding some hidden remainder of her in its vast archive.

He could not save what he could not reach. He could not prove that the voice beneath the floor had been hers.

But he had heard it.

“I’ll find you,” he said. “Whatever they left of you, I’ll find it.”

The lattice in his body answered with a tremor. Through the walls, the station opened pathways of scent and heat. The fungal growth beside the door bent away, exposing a narrow maintenance seam.

He understood the invitation.

Or the trap.

The Faculty was coming, and the thing inside him had begun to learn the shape of the place.

He gathered Mira against him. His left hand remained human enough to cradle her skull. His right curled into blackening claws.

When he stood, the pump room shuddered in recognition.

Above the door, something whispered through the pipes in a language made of hunger.

Vance carried Mira toward it.

chapters.title: The Hive Collapse
chapters.text:
Vance carried Mira through the seam in the pump-room wall.

The opening closed behind them with a wet contraction of fungal tissue. Beyond it, the station narrowed into service passages ribbed with metal and pale growth. Heat moved through the walls. Electrical current glittered beneath the floor. Every surface seemed to breathe.

Mira’s head rested against his shoulder. Her pulse tapped faintly beneath her throat.

“The food,” she whispered.

“I know.”

He moved silently. His altered joints bent too far, then corrected themselves. Claws found seams in the walls and held him where a human body would have slipped. Behind them, drones battered the sealed room. Their commands reached him through the station’s living systems:

Preserve. Contain. Return.

Vance opened the vents in his altered body.

A bitter pheromone mist spread through the passage. The nearest fungal mats recoiled. A hatch unlocked. Farther behind him, the drones slowed, their limbs twitching as the orders became confused.

Not command, he thought. Interference.

He descended into a dormitory carved from an old subway tunnel. Rows of narrow beds filled the chamber. People lay beneath gray blankets, some awake, some too weak to move. Their faces turned upward as Vance dropped from the ceiling.

A woman screamed. A man raised a broken feeding cup.

“It’s all right,” Vance said.

His voice rasped through the new structures in his throat. It sounded almost human.

Mira stirred. “The food.”

The survivors stared at her, then at his armored face.

“You’re not one of them,” someone said.

“No,” Vance answered, though the word felt less certain than it once had. “But I know how to open doors.”

The dormitory controls were embedded in a column of living tissue. His blood and scent gave the system permission. Locks withdrew. Doors clanged open along the tunnel, revealing stairwells and storage rooms where more patients had been confined.

People began to crawl out.

Some could walk. Some had to be carried. Vance pointed them toward the upper routes, away from the Faculty’s elevators. He told them to follow the emergency lights. He did not tell them that the surface might be worse than the station.

A child clung to her mother’s coat and looked at his claws.

“Are you a doctor?”

Vance looked down at Mira.

“I was.”

He left the survivors moving upward and followed the taste of power through the walls. The nutrient vats lay beneath the dormitory, behind a pressure door. He cut through its lock.

Inside, tanks rose in rows, each filled with dark red slurry. Agitators turned beneath translucent lids. The air smelled of iron, salt, and preserved tissue.

Vance placed his claws against the main conduits.

The station’s current poured through him. For an instant he felt every pump, freezer, and neural relay drawing power from the buried grid. Then he changed the flow.

The vats ruptured.

Lids blew into the ceiling. Warm fluid cascaded across the floor and flooded the electrical channels. Lights burst overhead. Pumps shrieked. Far above, doors opened and slammed in frantic sequence as the station shuddered.

The command-grammar broke apart.

Feed became drown. Preserve became release. Hold became flee.

Vance turned toward the Synapsis Chamber.

He found it by following the Pattern’s pain.

The chamber doors stood open. Beneath its transparent floor, the Pattern writhed through black fluid and silver filaments. Faces surfaced and vanished. Voices crowded the air: surgical oaths, prayers, names repeated until they lost meaning.

Mira’s voice was among them.

Please don’t let them.

At the chamber’s center, Provost Malkus and Archivist Seraphine stood within a ring of machinery. Silver lace extended from the apparatus into a body suspended above the Pattern. Needles crowned its opened skull.

The identity being transferred was a composite of stolen memories, another mind for the Faculty to inhabit.

Seraphine turned. “You have damaged the process.”

Vance stepped into the light with Mira in his arms. “You damaged the people.”

Malkus smiled, his mouth opening in layered plates. “Person, body, memory—temporary arrangements.”

Silver lace snapped toward Vance.

He caught the first filament and tore it free. It burned through his palm. The body in the cradle convulsed, and voices erupted from below.

Vance seized another strand, then another. The neural lace wrapped his arms and chest, searching for the access points in his scarred flesh. He pulled until the silver mesh parted with a wet, singing sound.

Malkus attacked.

The Provost unfolded into a mass of limbs. A hooked arm struck Vance across the chamber and drove him into a console. Chitin cracked along his ribs. Malkus regenerated even as he moved, torn tissue crawling together beneath his carapace.

“You were made for this,” Malkus hissed. “Your consent remains in the original record.”

“My consent was not a blank check.”

Malkus raised both arms. Blades pushed through his flesh.

Something slammed into him from the side.

Imago.

The doctor’s body was crushed beneath the Provost’s weight, one arm twisted backward, his thorax split and leaking clear fluid. Still, he held Malkus’s killing limbs away from Vance.

Imago looked at him. One eye had burst. The other was strangely gentle.

“I was a doctor once too,” he murmured.

Malkus tore free and struck him through the abdomen.

Imago sagged but did not release him.

Vance rose.

He could feel the Pattern as a wound beneath the world. Mira’s fragment trembled within it. The consumed minds pressed against one another, preserved and starving.

At the center pulsed a node of silver tissue and black nerve—the oldest command, the engine’s heart.

The Pattern opened around him.

Vance drove both claws into the core.

Every voice screamed.

He pulled the node apart.

The Pattern convulsed. Silver filaments whipped through the chamber. Seraphine lifted from the floor and vanished into the black fluid, shouting that the archive must survive. Malkus staggered as his regenerative flesh collapsed faster than it could repair.

The station began to hemorrhage.

Black nutrient fluid burst from the walls. Fungal columns split. Pipes ruptured overhead. The floor buckled as the machinery lost its sustaining intelligence.

Vance found Mira and dragged her into his arms.

Behind him, Imago lay half-submerged in the spreading dark. Vance looked back once.

The doctor’s remaining eye followed him.

“Go,” Imago said.

The escape shaft yawned open at the end of the chamber. Vance climbed into it with Mira against his chest. Below, the Eternal Faculty’s engine screamed through every failing speaker, a thousand stolen minds crying out as one.

He pulled himself upward.

The shaft shook. Fluid rose beneath them.

Vance tightened his claws around Mira and climbed toward the thin promise of open air while the buried laboratory died below.

chapters.title: Emergence
chapters.text:
The shaft narrowed above them.

Vance climbed sideways, Mira secured against his chest with torn conduit. Each movement dragged fire through his ribs. Beneath the pain came other sensations: groundwater seeping through stone, the tremor of fleeing bodies somewhere above, current flickering in a buried cable.

And beneath everything, the Pattern screamed.

It no longer needed speakers. Its death passed through his altered nerves, thousands of minds slipping from their chambers into silence. Most had become pressure without words. Others remained terribly distinct.

Water.

Mother.

Please, doctor.

He climbed.

Mira’s head rested against his collarbone. Blood had stiffened her hair. Her eyes remained closed, but every few minutes her lips moved.

“The food.”

He tightened his arm around her.

“I know, Mira.”

His voice resonated strangely inside the new cavities of his throat.

A tremor shook dust from the shaft. Far below, something immense collapsed. The emergency lights vanished in succession, leaving him suspended above a darkness his changed senses could still penetrate: roots contracting, fluids draining, doors struggling through their final commands.

Preserve.

Then, fainter:

Release.

He remembered Imago holding Malkus back, his abdomen split, his dying strength spent on a man he had helped prepare for slaughter.

Go.

Vance drove his claws into the concrete and climbed.

The marks disturbed him. These hands had once tied sutures, examined pupils, rested reassuringly on frightened shoulders. Now black talons found purchase where human fingers would have failed.

Above him, a thin gray radiance entered the shaft.

Dawn.

He braced his feet, pushed against a fractured slab, and forced a passage through the earth. Wind struck his face, smelling of ash and wet stone.

For several seconds he knelt without moving.

The megacity lay in broken layers. Towers leaned together above streets buried under their own facades. Bridges hung between buildings that no longer possessed foundations. Swollen silver growth covered vents, windows, the open mouths of overturned vehicles.

Beyond them, sunlight spread through a veil of cloud, turning the horizon copper.

He had seen this city from a cracked viewport. It had looked dead. Standing inside it, he could feel how much still lived here.

None of it promised mercy.

He lowered Mira onto fallen masonry. Plates along his ribs shifted with each breath. The sensory pits beneath his cheekbones registered her warmth, but he distrusted the effortless certainty of that knowledge.

He placed two claws gently against her throat.

A pulse. Weak, but regular.

“Stay with me.”

She did not answer.

For a moment he remembered examining another woman beside a sunlit window. He knew the room’s wallpaper, the smell of boiled linen, the ache in his knees.

He had never been in that room.

The memory dissolved, leaving someone else’s grief behind.

Vance pressed his forehead against the cold stone until it passed. The Pattern was dying, but fragments of its contents had lodged in him. He could not tell whether he had rescued anything or merely carried the wreckage out.

Mira’s lips parted.

He leaned closer.

“The food,” she whispered.

He waited for another word. There was none.

Searching the rubble for cloth, he found a medical bag wedged beneath a collapsed wall. Its leather was cracked; mold furred the clasp. He worked it free and opened it with awkward care.

Most of the instruments had rusted together. A glass vial broke beneath his touch. But one roll of bandages remained sealed, and a diagnostic hammer lay intact beneath the debris.

He lifted the hammer. Its curved metal returned a warped reflection: one recognizable eye, dark plates climbing his temple, pits opening beneath the cheekbone.

He turned it over.

A bag would not restore him. Yet when he eased its strap over his shoulder, he knew what to do next.

He wrapped Mira’s torn scalp, checked the dressing, and freed her from the conduit before lifting her again.

“We’ll find a way to be human again,” he whispered.

His claws clicked against each other.

The promise had escaped him before he could examine it. He could not give Mira back the mind the Faculty had taken. He could not even name everything moving beneath his own skin. A second rhythm stirred under his sternum; the fungal veins below the pavement offered themselves to senses he had never possessed.

He adjusted his grip so no sharp edge touched her.

Behind him, the ground subsided. Black vapor rose from the shaft, carrying a last thin confusion of voices. He thought he heard Imago. He thought he heard Mira.

Then the wind scattered them.

Beyond the broken avenues stood a low ruin whose upper floors remained intact. A thread of smoke lifted from its roof.

People, perhaps. Shelter. Another appetite.

Vance started toward it.

The medical bag struck his hip with every step. He would never again be the man who had entered the ice. Whatever waited ahead would see that before it heard his name.

Mira was warm against his chest.

He carried her into the ruined light, monstrous and afraid, keeping his claws turned away from her, holding what remained of hope.

prompt: Imagine a story where a war veteran who’s been deaf for years suddenly hears a stranger’s voice again and must unravel why it’s tied to his lost past. Focus on themes of isolation, redemption, and the unexpected price of regained senses. Set it in a crumbling urban hospital and the shadowed backstreets of a modern Middle Eastern city.

chapters.title: The Corridor of Static
chapters.text:
Adam Khalil knew the city through his feet.

Buses made the pavement tremble before they appeared. Water pipes shuddered in the walls when the generator started. Even the old apartment building announced its movements through vibration: a stair creaking, a door slamming, a truck grinding along the avenue below.

Sound belonged to other people.

For seven years Adam had lived behind glass. He could read lips in three languages and understand a conversation from hands, posture, and expression. He could feel a shout through a tabletop or recognize an approaching motorcycle by the tremor it sent through the pavement. But the world reached him incomplete, stripped of its voice.

He had learned to live with that absence.

He had not learned to stop watching for danger.

That morning, he shaved beside the bathroom mirror and touched the pale scar behind his left ear. The doctors had called it blast trauma, permanent nerve damage. They had been very certain. Adam had been twenty-eight then. He was thirty-five now.

The public hospital had summoned him for a routine examination. Routine, he had learned, was a word institutions used when they had forgotten why they were touching you.

He put the appointment slip in his pocket, checked his phone, and walked outside.

The old quarter was already hot. Vendors arranged oranges beneath patched umbrellas. A traffic officer argued with a man in a gray robe. Their mouths opened and closed, their hands cutting the air. Adam kept moving.

The hospital leaned over the street like a tired animal. Its balconies were cracked, its walls stained by exhaust and old rain. Inside, the air smelled of disinfectant, damp plaster, and boiled vegetables. A ceiling fan turned above the reception desk, its chipped blades casting a broken shadow.

Adam showed the clerk his papers. She spoke without looking up.

He pointed to his ear.

With an irritated sigh, she wrote the department number on a scrap of paper.

Second floor.

The stairwell was crowded. Adam climbed with one hand on the railing, feeling footsteps travel through the metal. On the landing, orderlies carried a stretcher past him. A woman followed, gripping the hand of a boy whose mouth was wide with crying.

Adam looked away.

The second-floor corridor was packed with patients. Men sat beneath peeling health posters. Women held folders in their laps. A child slept across his mother’s knees. Fluorescent tubes flickered overhead, making the crowd move in broken frames.

Adam found a place beside a dusty window.

Once, he had carried voices across borders. As a military translator, he had made orders understandable and pleas impossible to ignore. His mouth had been a bridge between strangers.

Then the bridge had collapsed.

A man in a brown jacket emerged from the crowd near the nurses’ station. Adam noticed him because he moved against the flow. He was tall but stooped, with close-cropped hair and a pale scar running from the corner of his mouth into his cheek.

The man’s gaze passed over Adam, then returned.

Recognition stirred in Adam, though he could not place the face.

The stranger came closer. His left hand was curled tightly at his side.

He seemed to be passing. His shoulder brushed Adam’s.

His lips moved.

Adam saw one word.

Barqa.

Sound broke open.

It struck him as if the hospital had exploded inside his skull. The fluorescent lights buzzed. Shoes scraped across the tile. A metal tray clattered somewhere nearby. A monitor beeped. Voices rose over one another, indistinct and furious. Someone was praying. A nurse shouted for a doctor.

Then the child began to scream.

Adam clapped his hands over his ears, but the sound only grew louder. He heard his own breath rasping, the pounding of his heart, the harsh machinery beneath the building. Every noise arrived at once, sharp enough to cut.

The scarred man was walking away.

Adam pushed into the crowd. He saw the brown jacket near the stairwell, then behind three men, then gone. He seized a stranger’s sleeve.

“What?” the man demanded.

The word struck Adam like a blow.

His knees buckled.

The corridor tilted beneath him. Lights burst white across his vision. The child was still screaming. Someone called his name.

Then the floor rose and swallowed him.

He woke in a narrow examination room with a doctor leaning over him. The doctor’s mouth moved rapidly. A nurse loosened Adam’s collar and pressed fingers to his wrist.

Adam pointed to his ears.

The doctor spoke again, slower.

“Can you hear me?”

The shape of the question reached Adam, but not its sound.

He shook his head.

They tested his pupils, blood pressure, and reflexes. They drew blood. A machine was rolled into the room and cold instruments pressed against his chest. Adam tried to explain about the stranger, about the word, about the torrent of noise, but every explanation failed in his hands.

He wrote on the back of his appointment slip:

I heard.

The doctor read it and frowned. Beneath the sentence, he wrote:

You are deaf.

Adam stared at the words.

By late afternoon, they released him. No stroke. No seizure. No visible injury. A physician recommended rest and an appointment with an ear specialist, as though a specialist could locate seven years of silence and explain why it had vanished for less than a minute.

Outside, the city looked unchanged.

Traffic pushed through the avenue. Vendors waved customers toward their stalls. A motorcycle cut across the pavement. Adam saw everything and heard nothing.

Silence had returned, settling over him with its old, familiar weight.

At home, he sat on the edge of his bed without removing his shoes. A truck passed below, sending a faint tremor through the building. Dust drifted from the ceiling.

His phone lit with a message from the hospital reminding him about his next appointment.

Adam deleted it.

In the bathroom, he stood before the mirror and touched the scar behind his ear. His face looked hollow and older than it had that morning.

The stranger’s lips moved again in memory.

Barqa.

The word had not been spoken to him in years. Not by anyone who knew what it meant.

A village. A road. A line of names he had buried so deeply that even memory had stopped searching.

Adam lowered his hand.

The silence remained, but it no longer felt sealed. Somewhere inside it, a door had opened.

The stranger had disappeared.

The word had not.

It burned in the dark behind Adam’s ears.

chapters.title: The Dead Man's Room
chapters.text:
Adam returned to the hospital with the word **Barqa** written three times on the inside of his wrist.

He had slept badly. Whenever he closed his eyes, the stranger’s mouth appeared again: the pale scar running from it into his cheek, the careful shape of the whispered word. Adam had searched Barqa before dawn. It was a village beyond the eastern hills, a road on an old military map, and nothing else. No explanation for why the word had broken through seven years of silence.

The hospital was already crowded. Relatives filled the corridors; orderlies pushed carts between them; a child clung to his mother’s dress. Adam knew the movement of the place by sight and vibration. He ignored the stares and went directly to the corridor where the stranger had passed him.

There was no one there.

Adam stopped beneath the fluorescent lights. He remembered the sudden flood of sound—the buzzing tubes, shoes scraping tile, a clattering tray, the scream of a child. Now the corridor was mute again.

He looked up.

The security camera above the nurses’ station had been smashed. Another camera near the stairwell hung from its wires, turning slightly in the draft.

A nurse in a green coat passed with a stack of files. Adam stepped into her path and sketched a face in the air: close-cropped hair, a scar beside the mouth. Then he wrote in his notebook:

*The man who was here yesterday. Brown jacket.*

The nurse read it. Recognition crossed her face.

“Room three-twelve,” she said.

Adam caught the words from her lips.

She pointed toward the elevators. “He visited the old man.”

“Who?”

“Rashid Mansour.” She tapped the file. “He died last night.”

Adam pointed toward the stairwell and wrote, *Why did the scarred man visit him?*

The nurse’s expression tightened. “Ask Nadia. Records office. His daughter.”

She started away, but Adam caught her sleeve. He wrote, *What happened?*

The nurse glanced down the corridor before answering.

“He was sick for a long time. Kept asking for people who weren’t there.”

Then she freed herself and disappeared behind the swinging doors.

Adam took the stairs.

Room 312 was at the far end of a dim ward. A paper sign on the door read:

**MANSOUR, R. — RELEASED TO MORGUE**

The door stood open.

Inside, the bed had been stripped. A gray blanket lay folded at its foot, and a plastic cup rested on the bedside table beside a comb tangled with white hair. Adam searched the drawer, then the cabinet. Nothing.

He crouched and slid his fingers beneath the mattress.

They touched cloth.

The notebook was black, its cover softened by years of use. Adam carried it to the window and opened it beneath the weak daylight.

The first pages contained columns of dates and initials.

**K-17 — transferred.**  
**Haddad, J. — no confirmation.**  
**S-4 — paid in full.**  
**Barqa — 06/11.**

Names had been crossed out or circled until the paper tore. Between the lists, sentences appeared in Arabic and English:

*They said the order came from above.*

*Not soldiers. Witnesses.*

Then, underlined twice:

**MERIDIAN SOLUTIONS**

Adam knew the name. Meridian supplied security teams and vehicles to governments that preferred their violence at a distance. He knew the logo too: a silver compass inside a black square.

He turned the page.

A crude map filled the center spread. A road curved around a cluster of buildings. Beside it, in block letters, someone had written **BARQA**.

Beneath the map was a list of names.

One stopped Adam’s hand.

**Jawad Haddad.**

He had seen that name carved into a military cemetery three years earlier. His squadmate. Listed dead in the same operation that had taken Adam’s hearing.

A pressure gathered behind his eyes. Dust. Heat. A man shouting with his mouth open.

The door moved.

A woman stood in the opening, holding a file against her ribs. She was around thirty, with dark hair pulled into a loose knot and the exhausted face of someone who belonged to the hospital more than the city outside.

Her eyes went to the notebook.

Adam rose.

She closed the door behind her. She did not call security.

“You are Adam Khalil,” she said.

He nodded.

“Nurse Salma told me you would come.”

Adam pointed to the notebook, then to the empty bed. He drew the stranger’s scar with one finger and wrote:

*He visited your father. He said a word to me yesterday.*

“What word?”

Adam turned the notebook around.

**BARQA.**

The woman’s grip tightened on the file.

“My father said it too,” she said. “Before he died.”

Adam stared at her.

She sat on the edge of the bed. “He had failing lungs, but that wasn’t what frightened me. He stopped sleeping. Kept asking who had come through the door. There was no one.”

She touched the black cover.

“My father was a field medic. Army first, then contractors. He never told me where he worked. When I was young, he woke screaming. Later, he stopped screaming and began writing.”

Adam opened the notebook to the Meridian logo.

Nadia looked at it and went pale. “I know that mark.”

He tapped the name Haddad, then wrote:

*Who is he?*

“I don’t know.”

Adam wrote, *He is dead.*

“That is not an answer.”

He closed the notebook. His fingers had begun to shake.

Nadia looked toward the corridor. “If you take that, people will know.”

“Who?”

Her mouth twisted. “That is what I’ve been trying to find out.”

For a moment, they faced each other across the stripped bed. Outside, bodies moved soundlessly past the glass: doctors, cleaners, families waiting for news.

Nadia reached into her pocket and took out a small brass key.

“I can access the old hospital records,” she said. “My father’s employment files. Transfers. Anything they failed to remove.”

Adam wrote, *Why help me?*

She looked at the bed.

“Because he spent his life refusing to tell me what happened. At the end, he held my hand and apologized to someone who wasn’t there.”

She stood.

“Come tomorrow. After sunset. Records basement.”

Adam slipped the notebook beneath his coat.

At the door, Nadia spoke again. He turned.

Her lips formed the question slowly.

“Do you hear him?”

Adam shook his head.

Outside, the city struck him in fragments.

His own name, whispered close to his ear.

A distant siren.

Then a woman weeping, so softly he could not tell whether she was in the street or inside his skull.

The sounds vanished. Silence settled over him again.

Adam stood beneath the hospital’s cracked façade, one hand pressed against the notebook, and understood that the silence had begun to crack with him.

chapters.title: Barqa
chapters.text:
Adam’s apartment had one room, one window, and no reason for anyone to visit.

He locked the door and stood with his back against it, watching the city move beyond the glass. Traffic crawled along the avenue in red and white threads. He could not hear the horns, engines, or arguments passing between balconies. He saw them instead: mouths opening, hands rising, bodies leaning toward one another with the exhausted urgency of people who believed volume could change the world.

For seven years, silence had been a wall.

Tonight, it felt like a door that would not close.

He placed the black notebook on the table beside Nadia’s brass key and the scrap of paper on which he had written the word three times.

BARQA.

Under the yellow light, he opened the notebook.

The first pages were filled with names, dates, initials, and amounts of money. Some names had been crossed out so heavily the paper was torn. Adam recognized the habits of military records: compression, omission, the false neatness of men trying to make terrible things look administrative.

He copied the names into a clean column.

S. Qasim.  
H. Nasser.  
R. Mansour.  
J. Haddad.

He stopped.

The name seemed to change the air around it.

Jawad Haddad.

A memory stirred behind his eyes: a raised hand against a white sky, a crooked grin, boots sinking into dust. He reached for it, but it dissolved.

He turned the page.

A crude map filled the center spread. A road ran east from the hills, then divided around a cluster of small squares. A well was marked with an X. On the northern edge, someone had drawn a rectangle and written:

BARQA  
06/11

Beneath it, in English:

NOT SOLDIERS. WITNESSES.

Adam traced the words with his fingertip.

A pressure gathered behind his right eye. In the margin, Mansour had written a sentence in Arabic, then translated it below:

They said the order came from above.

Adam knew both languages. He did not know why his hands had begun to shake.

He leaned closer.

For less than a second, he heard a pen scratching paper.

Scratch. Scratch. Scratch.

The sound seemed to come from the table, though the pen beside his phone lay untouched. Adam stared at it. Silence returned.

He pressed his palms to his temples, then forced himself to turn another page.

Near the back were several photographs, most of them photocopies faded to gray. One showed Rashid Mansour in a field uniform, younger and broad-faced, standing beside a military truck. Another showed three men in desert gear beside a concrete barrier.

Adam recognized himself first.

He was twenty-five, thinner, his hair too long beneath his helmet. On his left stood a younger Jawad Haddad.

Adam touched the photograph.

Jawad had the same crooked mouth and deep-set eyes as the man in the hospital. His left hand rested against his thigh, the fingers already curled inward. There was no scar along his jaw then. His face was open, almost boyish.

Behind them, printed on the truck door, was a silver compass inside a black square.

Meridian Solutions.

Adam sat down.

The stranger’s eyes had been the same. So had the hand, the mouth, the way he had looked at Adam—not like a stranger, but like someone waiting for a locked door to open.

Jawad.

The name moved through him without sound.

Jawad was dead.

Adam knew this as surely as he knew his own name. The military record listed him as killed in the same operation that had taken Adam’s hearing. There had been a folded flag, perhaps a ceremony. Adam remembered a major speaking to Jawad’s mother and people touching his shoulder while he stood apart, unable to bear their pity.

But he did not remember a grave.

He searched the notebook again. On a page near the back, Jawad’s name appeared beside a date and one word:

CONFIRMED?

The question mark had been pressed so deeply it nearly pierced the paper.

Adam rose.

The cemetery lay beyond the western ring road, behind a wall stained black by exhaust and rain. He arrived after sunset and showed his old service identification to the guard, who barely glanced at it.

Inside, rows of white stones stretched beneath weak lamps. The city glimmered beyond the wall. Adam walked between the graves, reading names without seeing them, until he reached the military section for the Barqa operation.

JAWAD HADDAD  
TRANSLATOR’S AUXILIARY  
1988–2014

The stone was clean. Too clean. No flowers, photograph, or offering marked the earth around it.

Adam crouched and placed his palm against the marble.

For a moment, nothing happened.

Then the world cracked open.

A child’s face appeared in the dust, round and terrified, one cheek streaked with blood. Behind him stood villagers in a line. Someone shouted in English. Someone answered in Arabic. A rifle slammed against metal.

Adam smelled burning rubber.

A man called his name.

“Adam!”

The voice was young and furious.

Jawad.

Adam tore his hand from the grave.

Sound surged into him. Traffic beyond the wall became a river of grinding engines. Wind hissed through branches. Somewhere in the city, a woman laughed. From a distant minaret came the opening notes of the call to prayer, thin and mournful beneath the darkness.

His heart thudded once, twice, impossibly loud.

Then everything vanished.

Adam bent forward, gripping the stone as silence dropped over him again. Pain drove behind his eye, bright and pulsing. The memory remained: villagers, dust, the child’s face, Jawad calling him.

He fumbled for his phone and opened the notes application.

JAWAD IS ALIVE.

He stared at the sentence. It looked absurd, the desperate conclusion of a man whose mind had been damaged by war.

After a moment, he added:

OR SOMEONE WANTS ME TO THINK HE IS.

A scrape of gravel sounded at the edge of hearing.

Adam turned.

The path between the graves was empty.

Another scrape, closer.

He held his breath. Nothing followed. Only the pressure in his skull, the dark between the lamps, and the clean white stone beneath his hand.

Jawad Haddad had been buried ten years ago.

Yet Jawad was the man who had whispered Barqa.

Adam looked down at the name carved into the grave and understood that the dead man had spoken to him for a reason.

Now he had begun to remember why.

chapters.title: Shadowed Backstreets
chapters.text:
The visitor log had been written in a clerk’s cramped hand, each name squeezed into the margin beside the date.

Adam read it three times before the false name separated itself from the others.

**Kamal Darwish.**

The visitor had signed in just after midnight, the same night Rashid Mansour died. Beneath the name, impressed faintly into the paper, was the outline of a stamp: a circle divided by a diagonal line, with three Arabic letters inside.

Adam had seen the mark before.

It appeared on the last page of Mansour’s notebook, beside an address in the old quarter.

He copied the address, folded the paper, and slipped the notebook beneath his shirt.

The pharmacy had once been painted white. Its walls were now the color of old bone, and the green sign above the door was eaten with rust. Through the glass, shelves leaned beneath dusty boxes. A boy in a blue coat sat behind the counter reading a newspaper.

Adam stood across the street and watched.

No one entered. No one left.

The old quarter folded around the pharmacy in crooked layers: balconies sagging over alleys, shutters sealed against the sun, electrical wires knotted from wall to wall. There were streets in the city where the police came only when paid, streets where a person could vanish between one doorway and the next.

Adam crossed.

The boy looked up. Adam showed him the copied address.

The boy glanced at it, then at Adam, and shook his head.

Adam pointed toward the rear of the shop.

The boy shook his head again and returned to his newspaper.

A narrow passage ran along the building. Adam entered it, one hand brushing the wall. He read the place through vibration and pressure: a generator trembling behind brick, footsteps passing overhead, a door opening somewhere nearby.

At the passage’s end stood a wooden gate marked with the circular stamp.

The latch was open.

Beyond it lay a courtyard crowded with plastic chairs, rusted bicycles, and a blue water tank. A door stood ajar beneath a string of dead bulbs.

Adam stepped inside.

Something struck the back of his head.

White light burst across his vision. He dropped to one knee, clutching the notebook as it slipped from beneath his shirt.

A boot drove into his ribs.

The man above him wore a gray jacket and had a narrow face, a shaved scalp, and a fresh cut across one eyebrow. Behind him stood another man holding a length of pipe.

The first man pointed at Adam’s chest, then made a grabbing motion.

The notebook.

Adam shook his head.

The pipe came down. He rolled aside. Metal smashed the stones where his skull had been. He kicked backward, caught the gray-jacketed man behind the knee, and surged upright.

The second attacker seized his collar and slammed him into the wall.

Adam drove his forehead into the man’s nose. The grip loosened. He twisted free and ran through the open door.

Inside was a narrow room packed with sacks, broken furniture, and hanging laundry. He vaulted a crate, struck a table, and fell. The notebook skidded across the floor.

The gray-jacketed man appeared in the doorway.

Adam reached for it.

The man reached it first.

He bent, smiling.

A brown sleeve flashed across the room.

The stranger seized him by the throat and flung him into the doorframe. His head struck wood. He folded.

The second attacker lunged from behind. The stranger caught the pipe between both hands, wrenched it free, and drove an elbow into the man’s jaw. The pipe clattered away. One more short blow dropped him beside the sacks.

The stranger picked up the notebook and thrust it against Adam’s chest.

Adam saw the scar first: a pale seam running from the corner of the man’s mouth toward his cheek.

Then the eyes.

He had seen them in a photograph beside a military truck, young and laughing beneath a sky bleached white by dust.

Jawad.

Adam’s body recognized him before his mind could accept the name.

Jawad caught his wrist and pulled him through the rear of the room. They burst into an alley scarcely wide enough for their shoulders. Adam stumbled after him over damp stones. Jawad moved with a limp but no hesitation, turning beneath hanging sheets and through courtyards linked by broken walls.

A woman shouted from a window. Adam saw the anger in her face but heard nothing.

Jawad dragged him through a gap between two buildings and into a courtyard of shattered tiles. He released him.

Adam struck the wall with both palms.

**Jawad.**

The name formed silently on his lips. His mouth worked around all the questions that had waited seven years.

Jawad stood across the courtyard, breathing hard. His left hand was curled tight against his chest, the fingers drawn inward exactly as they had been in the photograph.

Adam pointed at him, then at himself.

Jawad shook his head.

“You don’t remember me.”

The words arrived without sound, read from the shape of his mouth. Yet beneath the movement came a faint impression, like a voice traveling through deep water.

Adam stepped forward.

“That’s what they wanted.”

A pulse began behind his eye.

He reached for Jawad’s sleeve. “Barqa.”

The word left him as a dry breath. Jawad flinched.

“I need you to remember.”

From the alley came movement. Adam turned toward it, then back.

Jawad was retreating through a doorway beneath a sagging arch.

Adam followed.

The passage was empty.

He searched the adjoining alley and the roofs above it. Nothing moved except a torn plastic bag snagged on wire. Jawad had vanished as completely as if the city had swallowed him.

Then the world broke open.

A groan rose behind Adam.

He spun. The gray-jacketed man crawled across the stones, clutching his throat. The second man rolled onto his back, making a wet, choking sound.

Adam heard it all.

The scrape of cloth. Loose gravel shifting beneath a palm. Water dripping from a pipe. His own breath tearing in and out of his chest.

Sound slammed into him.

Footsteps thundered beyond the walls. A motorbike shrieked past. Somewhere above, a metal shutter crashed down. His heart hammered with unbearable clarity.

Adam pressed both hands over his ears.

It made no difference.

The men groaned. He heard himself gasp. He heard the old quarter breathing through its cracks.

Jawad was alive.

And he was not the one hunting Adam.

That certainty should have brought relief.

Instead, Adam stood trembling in the filthy courtyard, the notebook clutched against his ribs, while the restored world screamed around him.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.text:
Adam woke to the smell of dust, iodine, and hot iron.

For several seconds he could not move. Cracks veined the ceiling above him, and morning light lay across a thin mattress on the wooden floor. His shoulder throbbed. His forearm burned where the pipe had struck.

Then he heard a needle pass through cloth.

The tiny tearing sound came again as someone drew thread through gauze.

Adam sat up.

The room lurched. The floorboards groaned beneath his hand. From below came a machine’s rapid clatter, a man shouting, then laughter rising through the ceiling in a distorted burst.

Jawad sat beside the mattress, his back against the wall. He had removed his brown jacket. His shirt was dark with sweat, and the scar along his jaw pulled pale when he bent his head. His left hand rested curled against his thigh, the fingers trembling.

“You’re awake,” he said.

The words reached Adam in fragments, rough and delayed, as though carried through a damaged radio.

Adam touched his ear. “Where?”

“Above a tailor shop. In the old quarter. They won’t look here.”

“Who are you?”

Jawad’s eyes hardened. “You know.”

“I know what your face resembles.”

“You know my face.”

Adam tried to stand. His knees gave way. Jawad caught him and lowered him back down.

The contact brought another burst of sound: cloth rubbing cloth, a breath close to his cheek, the wet click of a swallow.

Adam shoved him away.

Jawad let him.

Between them lay the black notebook, its pages swollen from the alley. A pistol rested beside it.

“Why did you save me?” Adam asked.

“Because they were going to kill you.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It’s the only one you’re ready for.”

Adam laughed, startled by the thin, ugly noise of his own voice. He had heard it only in broken flashes since the blast.

Jawad glanced toward the shuttered window. “The men at the pharmacy work for Meridian.”

The name tightened Adam’s chest.

“Meridian Solutions stopped being a security company years ago,” Jawad said. “They became whatever governments needed. Escorts. Interrogators. Cleaners.”

“Barqa,” Adam said.

Jawad nodded. “Barqa was a Meridian operation. They were attached to our unit as advisers, but when we entered the village, they took command.”

“I remember the village.”

“You remember pieces.”

“Villagers. A child. Weapons.”

“And an order.”

Adam looked at him.

“Sulaiman gave it,” Jawad said. “Every adult in the square. Then the houses. He claimed the village sheltered bomb makers. There was no bomb maker. No weapons cache.”

“Why kill them?”

“Because there were witnesses.”

The room seemed to contract. Beneath them, the tailor’s machine stopped.

Adam remembered the words in Mansour’s notebook.

“Not soldiers,” he said.

“Witnesses.”

Jawad leaned forward. “Mansour was our medic. He worked for Meridian before he understood what they were doing. After Barqa, he injected us with a suppressant. He said it would make the memories inaccessible.”

“Us?”

“You. Me. Two others who didn’t live long enough to tell anyone.”

Adam shook his head. “Memory suppressant.”

“Mansour called it that. He thought forgetting was better than being hunted.”

“Did it work?”

Jawad looked at him. “You lost seven years.”

Adam stared at his hands. They were shaking.

“During the escape,” Jawad continued, “an IED hit the convoy. You were thrown clear. The blast damaged your ears. I was trapped in the second vehicle.”

A picture stirred: orange light, a wheel turning slowly in the air, dust thick as smoke.

“Your body was never recovered,” Adam said.

“Meridian recovered me.”

Jawad’s curled hand trembled harder.

“They kept me alive to find out what I remembered. When I wouldn’t talk, they tried other methods. Later they left me in a drainage canal. Mansour found me and brought me to the city. He spent the rest of his life recording names.”

“And you let him die?”

“I arrived too late.”

“You were at the hospital.”

“Outside.”

“Why didn’t you come to me?”

Jawad’s face tightened. “You had built a life around not knowing.”

“What life?”

Neither answered.

The tailor’s machine began again below, its needle striking in quick, exact blows.

Adam watched the scar on Jawad’s face. “Show me.”

Jawad turned away.

“The scar.”

“Adam—”

“Show me.”

Light caught the ridges running from the corner of Jawad’s mouth toward his cheek. Adam reached out before fear could stop him.

His fingertip touched the scar.

The world broke open.

A truck burned in the road, its engine screaming. Smoke rolled across the village. A child crouched behind an overturned water jar, hands clamped over her mouth. Voices shouted in English and Arabic.

Jawad was inside the truck.

His face was younger, blood running from his hairline. His left hand clawed at the bent door.

“Adam!”

Adam stood outside with his rifle against his chest.

“Adam, don’t leave me!”

Behind him, someone shouted the order to fall back.

He turned.

He ran.

The memory widened. Jawad’s hand reached through the flames, fingers stretching toward him. The truck collapsed with a roar. Heat struck Adam’s back.

He pulled away from the scar and stumbled across the room.

“I left you,” he whispered.

Jawad said nothing.

“I heard you.”

“You couldn’t save me.”

“I heard you.”

The ringing inside Adam’s skull vanished.

Everything rushed in.

The tailor’s machine below. Jawad’s breathing. Water ticking through a pipe. A motorbike whining through the street. Fabric snapping beneath a blade. His own heart hammering, each beat vast and wet.

Then the city rose around him—horns, footsteps, vendors calling, a child crying somewhere beyond the walls. The sounds layered into a physical pressure that crushed his chest.

Adam clapped both hands over his ears.

It did nothing.

Jawad seized his shoulders. His mouth moved, but Adam could not separate the words from the flood.

The room filled with the burning truck.

With Jawad calling his name.

With the last thing Adam had chosen not to hear.

chapters.title: Meridian
chapters.text:
Meridian

By morning, Adam could hear the tailor’s machine through three floors of plaster.

Its needle clicked and paused, clicked and paused. Water moved in the pipes. A woman coughed below. Somewhere in the street, a truck changed gears.

He sat on the mattress with his palms over his ears. It made no difference.

“You should sleep,” Jawad said from the window.

Adam heard the words, the breath behind them, even the scrape of Jawad’s stubble as he turned.

“I slept for seven years.”

Jawad looked at him but did not answer.

Nadia arrived after sunrise carrying three paper cups of tea and a canvas bag. Her hands shook. Adam heard the tea trembling against the lids.

“You look worse,” she said.

“So do you.”

“I spent the night in the hospital basement.”

She set the bag down and removed a ledger wrapped in brown paper. Its cover was cracked and stained. Inside, columns of names, dates, dosages, and transfers filled the pages. Some names were crossed out. Others were marked in black:

SILENCED.

Adam recognized S. Qasim and H. Nasser from Rashid’s notebook. Beside each was a date and an injection amount. Jawad’s name appeared near the back, followed by a question mark and a torn strip of paper.

“My father kept this hidden in the records annex,” Nadia said. “It was filed under flood damage. There was no flood.”

Jawad stared at the ledger. “He worked for Meridian.”

“For eleven months,” Nadia said. “Not as a hospital employee. As a contractor medic.”

She turned a page. Rashid’s handwriting filled the margin.

*Memory suppression successful. Subject retains language and motor function. Emotional triggers unpredictable.*

Below it:

*Sound may return with memory.*

Adam pulled his hand away.

“He wasn’t only treating soldiers,” Nadia said. “He was recording what happened to them. Payments, transfers, people who disappeared afterward.”

“Why?” Jawad asked.

“Because he was afraid he’d forget.”

The tailor’s machine continued below them.

Nadia unfolded a photocopy. At the top was an address on the city’s western edge, beyond the old quarter and the scrapyards. Beneath it:

MERIDIAN SOLUTIONS—LOGISTICS AND SECURITY SERVICES.

“The notebook’s stamp belongs to Meridian,” she said. “This was a front office. Officially closed eight years ago. The utilities are still active.”

Jawad’s expression hardened. “Then they’re still working.”

Adam thought of the silver compass inside the black square. “I have something else.”

His storage locker was beneath the bus station, in a row of rusting metal boxes. He had not opened it in years. The key turned reluctantly.

Inside lay old uniforms, a water-damaged dictionary, photographs, and a black digital recorder no larger than a matchbox.

Adam lifted it.

The bus station roared around him. Engines coughed. Vendors shouted. A child cried near the ticket windows. Every sound entered his skull like a separate blow.

His thumb brushed the recorder’s cracked screen.

Heat.

Dust.

Diesel.

Then his own voice, younger and steady, speaking Arabic.

“Gather the civilians in the square. Separate the men from the women and children.”

A man answered in English, calm and close.

“Tell them it’s for their protection.”

Adam staggered.

His own voice continued.

“Tell them resistance will be treated as hostile action.”

A woman screamed.

Gunfire erupted—several shots, then a burst of static. Someone shouted Jawad’s name. A child began to cry.

The recorder fell from Adam’s hand.

When he returned to himself, he was on one knee. Nadia gripped his shoulder. Jawad stood before them with his pistol drawn, scanning the station.

“What did you hear?” Jawad asked.

“The order,” Adam said. His fingers closed around the recorder. “I translated it.”

“Then we have proof.”

“We have a damaged device.”

“We have your voice.”

Adam looked at him. “It could be altered.”

“By whom?”

“I don’t know.”

Jawad crouched in front of him. “You think I made this?”

“I think I don’t know what you made.”

The station seemed to narrow around them.

“You think I survived ten years to invent a story about you?” Jawad asked.

“I think you survived ten years by becoming someone I don’t know.”

Jawad looked away.

They took the recorder to Nadia’s apartment. She connected it to an old laptop. The file was damaged but readable. A jagged waveform appeared, breaking apart beneath static. The voices came in fragments, but the words remained clear enough.

Jawad leaned toward the screen. “Send it to someone.”

“Who?” Nadia asked. “Meridian threatens journalists, buys them, or buries them.”

“Send it to all of them.”

Adam stood by the window. His hearing had not faded. Traffic hissed below. A radio played in the neighboring flat. A dog barked several streets away. Pain pulsed behind his eye.

He wanted silence more than justice.

Nadia closed the laptop. “I need to return to the hospital. Rashid’s personnel file may identify his Meridian supervisor.”

“You’re not going back,” Jawad said.

“I work there.”

“They know you helped us.”

“They know nothing.”

A car door slammed in the street.

Adam looked down. Two men stood beside a gray sedan across from the hospital entrance. One wore a maintenance jacket. The other held a phone and watched the upper windows.

Adam recognized the shaved head and the cut through the eyebrow.

His hearing sharpened. He heard the phone vibrate in the man’s hand, the scrape of a shoe against pavement.

“They found the hospital,” Adam said.

Nadia reached for her coat.

Jawad caught her wrist. “No.”

“If they take the records—”

“They’re watching the entrance.”

“There’s a service door.”

A vehicle turned into the alley below. Then footsteps sounded in the stairwell.

One set.

Then two.

Jawad drew his pistol.

“Nadia,” he said, “the back window.”

She froze.

A fist struck the apartment door. The wood flexed. Adam heard a man outside say something too low for Nadia to catch.

He heard every syllable.

“Open up.”

The sound cut through him. He seized the recorder and closed his hand around it.

Jawad looked at him. “Can you move?”

Adam nodded, though the room tilted.

They climbed onto the narrow rear balcony as the door began to splinter. Below, the alley lay in shadow, cluttered with crates and rusted pipes. Nadia swung one leg over the railing.

Behind them, the lock gave way.

Adam heard the men enter.

He heard a weapon’s safety click off.

And beneath everything, faint but unmistakable, he heard his younger voice translating the order again.

chapters.title: The Day We Left
chapters.text:
The safety clicked.

Adam heard it as clearly as a bell beside his skull.

Nadia gasped. Jawad’s breath tightened. Behind them, the apartment door splintered under another blow.

And beneath those sounds, impossibly near, another voice continued speaking.

“Gather them in the square.”

His own voice.

Not the rough voice he used now, but the younger one preserved on the recorder: precise, obedient, carrying an order from one language into another.

Jawad gripped his shoulder. “Adam. Look at me.”

Adam did.

“Go,” Jawad said.

The door broke inward. A shot struck the wall. Nadia clutched the recorder to her chest as they moved toward the narrow balcony.

Then the city vanished.

Ten years earlier, Barqa lay beneath a white, pitiless sky.

The convoy entered the village shortly after noon: three armored trucks and a utility vehicle, all coated in dust. Adam sat between Jawad and Corporal Nasser, his translation kit knocking against his hip.

They had been told there was a bomb maker in the village, a man named Faris. The operation was supposed to be simple: search the houses, find the suspect, and leave.

Jawad leaned close. “You think there’s a bomb maker?”

“I think someone wanted us to come here.”

“That is not the same answer.”

The convoy stopped in the village square. Mud-brick houses pressed around it. A mosque with a green dome stood beyond the rooftops. Children watched from beside a wall, and women emerged from doorways, gathering their children behind them.

Then the Meridian vehicles arrived.

They had no national markings, only black squares bearing a silver compass. Four contractors climbed out wearing new body armor and carrying weapons cleaner than the soldiers’ rifles.

Their leader removed his sunglasses.

Adam remembered the narrow mouth and the silver watch. He did not know the man’s name yet.

The army captain approached him, received a folder, read it, and stepped away.

“Change of command,” the contractor said in English.

He turned to Adam. “You’re the translator?”

“Yes.”

“Then make yourself useful.”
